<!-- introthm-1: body_md -->
\label{theorem: arithmetic theorem in introduction}
    Let $F$ be a complex cubic field with complex embedding $\sigma_{\mathbb{C}}$. For a conductor ideal $\mathfrak{f}$, chosen so that the narrow ray class field $F^+(\mathfrak{f})$ is totally complex, denote by $\varepsilon$ a generator of the positive units congruent to $1$ modulo $\mathfrak{f}$ and write $\chi_{\varepsilon}$ for its characteristic polynomial. Let $\mathfrak{b}$ be any integral ideal coprime to $\mathfrak{f}$ and write $L=\mathfrak{f}\mathfrak{b}^{-1}$. Finally, consider an integral smoothing ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ such that $\operatorname{N}\mathfrak{a}$ is prime.
    
    If $\operatorname{N}\mathfrak{a}$ is coprime to $6\operatorname{N}(\mathfrak{f})\cdot \operatorname{disc}(\chi_{\varepsilon})$, then, for any admissible elements $h$ and $h'$:
    \begin{equation*}
        {\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h}(L) = {\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h'}(L).
    \end{equation*}
    In other words, for $\mathfrak{a}$ outside a finite set of primes, the complex number ${\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h}(L)$ is independent of $h$.
<!-- end introthm-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
We are calling $h$ admissible rather than $\lambda = hq$ for $q$ the positive generator of $\mathfrak{f}\cap\mathbb{Z}$ as in \cite{BCG23}. We recall the definition of admissibility in \eqref{eq: arithmetic admissible} below.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
The requirement that $\operatorname{N}\mathfrak{a}$ is coprime to $ \operatorname{disc}(\chi_{\varepsilon})$ is new to this paper and we highlight its role in the proof sketch of Theorem \ref{theorem: main theorem in main body}. For now, let us note that the consequence of excluding our smoothing ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ from a finite set of primes is relatively mild. After all, the complex numbers ${\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h}(L)$ depend only mildly on this choice. Indeed, for two smoothing ideals $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{c}$, we have the easily verifiable relation:
    \begin{equation*}
        \frac{{\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h}(L)^{\operatorname{N}\mathfrak{c}}}{{\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h}(\mathfrak{c}^{-1}L)}=\frac{{\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{c},h}(L)^{\operatorname{N}\mathfrak{a}}}{{\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{c},h}(\mathfrak{a}^{-1}L)}.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- introthm-2: body_md -->
\label{theorem: main result in introduction}
    Consider a pair of lattices $(V,L)$ with cyclic quotient $V/L \cong \mathbb{Z}/N$. Consider triples $h\in L\otimes\mathbb{Q}$, $\langle z\rangle \in \mathbb{P}(L^{\vee}\otimes\mathbb{C})-\mathbb{P}(L^{\vee}\otimes\mathbb{R}) $, and an automorphism $g$ of the pair $(V,L)$, which satisfy the following conditions:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $g\cdot h\equiv h$ modulo $L$.
        \item $\langle h\rangle_{\mathbb{Q}}$ generates the quotient $V/L$.
        \item $g\cdot \langle z\rangle =\langle z\rangle$.
    \end{itemize}
    Let $\chi_g$ denote the characteristic polynomial of $g$. If $(N,6\cdot \operatorname{disc} (\chi_g))=1$, then for all triples $(h,\langle z \rangle,g)$, $(h',\langle z \rangle,g)$ satisfying the conditions above such that $h\equiv h'$ modulo $L$, we have:
    \begin{equation*}
        \widetilde{\Phi}(h,\langle z \rangle,g) =  \widetilde{\Phi}(h',\langle z \rangle,g)
    \end{equation*}
    for the notation:
    \begin{equation*}
    \widetilde{\Phi}(h,\langle z \rangle,g)=\widetilde{\Gamma}_{a,ga}(z(h),z)=\frac{\Gamma_{a,ga}(z(h),z;L)^N}{\Gamma_{a,ga}(z(h),z;V)}
    \end{equation*}
    and the primitive functional $a\in V^{\vee} $ is determined by the triple.
<!-- end introthm-2 -->
<!-- conjecture-1: body_md -->
\label{conj: Stark L-functions}
    There exists a unit $u_{\mathfrak{f}}\in \mathcal{O}_{F^+(\mathfrak{f})}^*$ such that:
    \begin{equation*}
        L_{\mathfrak{f}}'(\chi,0) = -\frac{1}{e_{\mathfrak{f}}}\sum_{\sigma \in G} \chi(\sigma)\log|\iota (u_{\mathfrak{f}}^{\sigma})|^2
    \end{equation*}
    and for every place $w$ lying above a real place, we have $|u_{\mathfrak{f}}|_w=1$.
<!-- end conjecture-1 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The simplifying assumption $|S|\geq 3$ covers all non-trivial cases for complex cubic fields. Indeed, when $S$ contains two places that split completely, the Stark Conjecture is trivially true as all the $L$-functions vanish to order at least $2$ (except for the trivial character when $|S|=2$ - this case is dealt with separately) and so we may take $u_{\mathfrak{f}}=1$. In particular, for a non-trivial example, all the real places must ramify in $F^+(\mathfrak{f})$. For a complex cubic field with unique real embedding denoted by $\sigma_{\mathbb{R}}$, this is equivalent to:
    \begin{equation*}
        \operatorname{Cl}^+(\mathfrak{f}) \neq \operatorname{Cl}(\mathfrak{f})\iff \mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{f}}^{+,*} =\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{f}}^{*}
    \end{equation*}
    for the notation $ \mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{f}}^{+,*}=\{x\in 1+\mathfrak{f}\cap \mathcal{O}_{F}^*: \sigma_{\mathbb{R}}(x)>0\} $ and $\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{f}}^{*} =1+\mathfrak{f}\cap \mathcal{O}_{F}^* $. In particular, $\mathfrak{f}$ cannot be $(1)$ and so to obtain a non-trivial Stark unit, we must have $|S|\geq 3$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- conjecture-2: body_md -->
There exists a unit $u_{\mathfrak{f}}\in \mathcal{O}_{F^+(\mathfrak{f})}^*$ such that:
    \begin{equation*}
          \zeta_{\mathfrak{f}}'(\sigma,0) = -\frac{1}{e_{\mathfrak{f}}}\log|\iota (u_{\mathfrak{f}}^{\sigma})|^2
    \end{equation*}
    and for every place $w$ lying above a real place, we have $|u_{\mathfrak{f}}|_w=1$.
<!-- end conjecture-2 -->
<!-- conjecture-3: body_md -->
There exists a \emph{unique} unit $u_{\mathfrak{f},\mathfrak{a}}\in \mathcal{O}_{F^+(\mathfrak{f})}^*$ satisfying $u_{\mathfrak{f},\mathfrak{a}}-1\in \mathfrak{a}\mathcal{O}_{F^+(\mathfrak{f})}$ such that:
    \begin{equation*}
          \zeta_{\mathfrak{f},\mathfrak{a}}'(\sigma,0) = \log|\iota (u_{\mathfrak{f},\mathfrak{a}}^{\sigma})|^2
    \end{equation*}
    and for every place $w$ lying above a real place, we have $|u_{\mathfrak{f},\mathfrak{a}}|_w=1$. We call $u_{\mathfrak{f},\mathfrak{a}}$ \emph{the} $\mathfrak{a}$-smoothed Stark unit.
<!-- end conjecture-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
The change in rational constant is explained by the relation $u_{\mathfrak{f}}^{e_{\mathfrak{f}}}=u_{\mathfrak{f},\mathfrak{a}}^{\operatorname{N}(\mathfrak{a})-\sigma_\mathfrak{a}}$. We note that Stark's conjecture predicts that $u_{\mathfrak{f},\mathfrak{a}}^{\operatorname{N}(\mathfrak{a})-\sigma_\mathfrak{a}}$ is an $e_{\mathfrak{f}}$-th power in $F^+(\mathfrak{f})$ \cite[$\S4$ Lemma $6$]{Stark80}. The congruence condition ensures taking $e_{\mathfrak{f}}$-roots preserves uniqueness.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{theorem: limit formula}
    Let $F$ be a complex cubic field with fixed complex embedding $\sigma_{\mathbb{C}}$, $\mathfrak{f}$ a proper integral ideal and $\mathfrak{a}$ a prime ideal coprime to $6\operatorname{N}\mathfrak{f}$ and of prime norm. For $\mathfrak{b}$ integral ideal coprime to $\mathfrak{f}$, we let $L=\mathfrak{f}\mathfrak{b}^{-1}$. If we assume $\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{f}}^{+,*}=\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{f}}^*$, then the leading term of $\zeta_{\mathfrak{f},\mathfrak{a}}'(\sigma_{\mathfrak{b}},s)$ at $s=0$ is given by:
    \begin{equation*}
        \zeta_{\mathfrak{f},\mathfrak{a}}'(\sigma_{\mathfrak{b}},0)=\log|{\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h}(L)|^2
    \end{equation*}
    where $h\in L\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ is an admissible element: that is $h\equiv 1$ modulo $L$ and there exists a rational rescaling of $h$ which generates $\mathfrak{a}^{-1}L/L$.
    Explicitly, the analytic expression is a smoothed quotient of elliptic Gamma functions:
    \begin{equation*}
        {\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h}(L)^{-1} = \frac{\Gamma_{a,\varepsilon a}(\sigma_{\mathbb{C}}(h),\sigma_{\mathbb{C}};L)^{\operatorname{N}\mathfrak{a}}}{\Gamma_{a,\varepsilon a}(\sigma_{\mathbb{C}}(h),\sigma_{\mathbb{C}};V)}
    \end{equation*}
    where $\varepsilon$ is the unique generator of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{f}}^{+,*}$ that satisfies $\sigma_{\mathbb{R}}(\varepsilon)\in (0,1)$ for the unique real embedding and $a$ is a primitive functional on $L$ uniquely determined by the data $h$, $\sigma_{\mathbb{C}}$ and $\varepsilon$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- conjecture-4: body_md -->
The complex number ${\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h}(L) = \iota (u_{L,\mathfrak{a}})$ for $\iota : F^+(\mathfrak{f})\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ a complex embedding of the narrow ray class field extending $\sigma_{\mathbb{C}}$. Then:
\begin{itemize}
    \item The preimage is a unit, $\textbf{u}_{L,\mathfrak{a}}\in \mathcal{O}_{F^+(\mathfrak{f})}^*$.
    \item For every complex place $w$ extending the real embedding of $F$, we have $|\textbf{u}_{L,\mathfrak{a}}|_w=1$.
    \item Reciprocity law: for $\mathfrak{c}$ a fractional ideal coprime to $\mathfrak{f}$,  $\textbf{u}_{L,\mathfrak{a}}^{\sigma_{\mathfrak{c}}}= \textbf{u}_{\mathfrak{c}^{-1}L,\mathfrak{a}}$.
\end{itemize}
Moreover, the complex number ${\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h}(L)$ is independent of $h$.
<!-- end conjecture-4 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
We now give an example of this phenomenon. Consider the complex cubic field $F=\mathbb{Q}(\beta)$ for $\beta^3-\beta^2+3\beta-4=0$, viewed as a subfield of $\mathbb{C}$ by specifying $\beta\in \mathbb{H}$. Above the rational primes $p\in\{2,3,7\}$, we have a unique prime ideal of norm $p$, which we denote $\mathfrak{p}_p$. We choose our conductor ideal to be $\mathfrak{f}=\mathfrak{p}_3$; this has narrow ray class group $\operatorname{Cl}^+(\mathfrak{f})\cong\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$, generated by $\mathfrak{b}= \mathfrak{p}_2$. Finally, take as our smoothing ideal $\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{p}_7$.

    For $L=\mathfrak{f}$, the following are two admissible elements:
    \begin{equation*}
        h = \beta^2 + 3\beta + 15 \quad \quad h' = 11\beta^2 + 5\beta + 46.
    \end{equation*}
    Write $\Gamma^N(z,\tau,\sigma) = \frac{\Gamma(z,\tau,\sigma)^N}{\Gamma(Nz,N\tau,N\sigma)}$ for the $N$-smoothed Gamma function. Here $N=\operatorname{N}\mathfrak{a}=7$. Then:
    \begin{align*}
        {\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h}(L)^{-1}&= \Gamma^N\left(\frac{1}{3},\frac{-\beta-52}{168},\frac{-\beta^2+16}{168}\right) \approx -4.336094 -1.464725i
        \\ {\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h'}(L)^{-1}&= \Gamma^N\left(\frac{1}{3},\frac{-\beta-10}{189},\frac{-\beta^2-89}{189}\right)\cdot \Gamma^N\left(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{-\beta^2-\beta-99}{378},\frac{-\beta-10}{189},\frac{-\beta^2-89}{189}\right)\approx -4.336094 -1.464725i
    \end{align*}
   which numerically verifies the equality ${\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h}(L)={\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h'}(L)$. 
   
   As an aside, recall that this complex number (conjecturally) equals $\iota(u_{\mathfrak{f},\mathfrak{a}})$ for a complex embedding $\iota:F^+(\mathfrak{f})\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$. To compute this Stark unit precisely, we use the (conjectured) reciprocity law: that is to say, the algebraic conjugates of $u_{\mathfrak{f},\mathfrak{a}}$ are given by ${\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h}(L)$ for $L=\mathfrak{f}\mathfrak{b}^{-j}$, $j\in \{0,1,2,3\}$. Then, using the \texttt{algdep} functionality of Pari-GP, we deduce that $u_{\mathfrak{f},\mathfrak{a}}$ is a root of the following polynomial:
    \begin{equation*}
        f(x)=x^4 - (1-\beta)\cdot x^3+(6\beta^2 - 2\beta - 5)\cdot x^2-(1-\beta)\cdot x+1\in \mathcal{O}_{F}[x].
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
Since the Stark conjecture is trivial in the case that $S$ contains at least two places that split completely in $F^+(\mathfrak{f})$, the only other class of cases is when $F$ is totally real. In this case, there is now a choice for which place splits completely, namely whether it is archimedean or finite. Progress in the totally real case when the archimedean place splits dates back to the work of Shintani \cite{Shintani76}; for recent work in the real quadratic field case, see the work of Kopp \cite{Kopp25} and breakthrough paper of Radchenko-Wheeler \cite{Radchenko26}. The finite prime case has recently been proven in the groundbreaking work of Dasgupta-Kakde \cite{DK_Brumer,DK_Z}; see also \cite{DK24} for the implications for the Gross-Stark conjecture and explicit class field theory for totally real fields. To appreciate the distinct flavours of the archimedean and finite place formulations, consider the case of $\mathbb{Q}$: in the archimedean setting, this is the theory of cyclotomic units; in the finite setting, Stark's conjecture follows from Stickelberger's Theorem.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
For a positive integer $N$, we have the following functional identities:
    \begin{align}
        \prod_{j=0}^{N-1}\Gamma_n\left(z+\frac{j}{N},\tau_0,\dots,\tau_n\right) &= \Gamma_n(Nz,N\tau_0,\dots,N\tau_n) \label{eq: first DR}
        \\ \prod_{j=0}^{N-1}\Gamma_n(z+j\tau_i,\tau_0,\dots,N\tau_i,\dots,\tau_n) &= \Gamma_n(z,\tau_0,\dots,\tau_i,\dots,\tau_n) \label{eq: second DR}
    \end{align}
    Combining these two, yields the pushforward relation:
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: general pushforward}
           \prod_{j,j_0,\dots, j_n=0}^{N-1}\Gamma\left(z+\frac{j+j_0\tau_0+\cdots+j_n\tau_n}{N},\tau_0,\dots,\tau_n\right)=\Gamma(Nz,\tau_0,\dots,\tau_n).
    \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
In homogeneous coordinates, the action of $G_3$ is given by:
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: homogeneous action}
        (l,g)\cdot (w,z) = (w-gz(l),gz).
    \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
If $\frac{v}{z(v)}$ trivialises $\mathcal{O}(1)$ over $U$, then $\frac{gv}{gz(gv)}=\frac{gv}{z(v)}$ trivialises $\mathcal{O}(1)$ over $V$. If we let $w=z(u)\in \mathbb{C}$, then with respect to these trivialisations, the action becomes:
   \[\begin{tikzcd}
	{(u,\langle z\rangle )} && {(gu - l,\langle gz\rangle )} \\
	{(w,z)} && \begin{array}{c} (gz(gu)-gz(l),gz)=(w-gz(l),gz) \end{array}
	\arrow[maps to, from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[tail reversed, from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[tail reversed, from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow[maps to, from=2-1, to=2-3]
\end{tikzcd}\]
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def: open cover}
    Our open cover of $X_3$ is $\mathcal{U}=\{V_a\}_{a\in \Lambda_{\text{prim}}}$ for $V_a = (\mathbb{C}\times U_a)/\mathbb{C}^*$ and $U_a$ defined by:
    \begin{equation*}
        U_a = \{z \in \Lambda\otimes\mathbb{C}-\mathbb{C}\cdot \Lambda\otimes\mathbb{R}: z(\lambda)/z(\mu)\in \mathbb{H} \text{ for }\lambda\wedge\mu \text{ oriented basis of }\ker(a)\otimes\mathbb{Q}\}
    \end{equation*}
    The orientation on $\ker(a)$ is that induced by $v\wedge -:\bigwedge^2\ker(a)\xrightarrow{\sim}\bigwedge^3L\cong \mathbb{Z}$ for any $v$ satisfying $a(v)>0$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
Notice that $V_a$ is biholomorphic to $ \mathbb{C}\times \pi(U_a)$ and $\pi(U_a)$ is biholomorphic to $\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{H}$. In particular, the opens $V_a$ are contractible domains of holomorphy,
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
We give a geometric interpretation of the open $V_a$. Recall that primitive functionals are in bijection with oriented planes in $L\otimes\mathbb{Q}$, via the correspondence $a\mapsto \ker(a)$ and the orientation described in Definition \ref{def: open cover}.
    
    We now claim that any oriented plane $P$ in $L\otimes\mathbb{R}$ determines a contractible domain of holomorphy in $\mathbb{P}(\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{C})-\mathbb{P}(\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{R})$. To see this, recognise that $\mathbb{P}(\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{C})-\mathbb{P}(\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{R})$ is fibered over the Grassmannian of oriented planes $\operatorname{Gr}_2^+(\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{R})\cong S^2$ with fibers biholomorphic to $\mathbb{H}$. An oriented plane $P$ in $ L\otimes\mathbb{R}$ determines a loop $S^1$ inside $\operatorname{Gr}_2^+(\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{R})$ by considering lines in a complementary plane to $(L/P)^{\vee}\otimes\mathbb{R}\cong \mathbb{R}$. The orientation allows us to single out one of the two discs in $S^2-S^1$. The corresponding open of $\mathbb{P}(\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{C})-\mathbb{P}(\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{R})$ obtained by taking the preimage is clearly contractible and a domain of holomorphy. This open consists of those functionals that restrict to an isomorphism $P\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb{C}$ and further satisfy an orientation condition.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a $G_3$-equivariant sheaf of abelian groups on $X_3$. For a $G_3$-invariant open cover $\mathcal{U}$, we form the double complex:
    \begin{equation*}
        C_{G_3}^{p,q}(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{F}) = C^p(G_3,\check{C}^q(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{F})) \quad \quad C^n_{G_3}(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{F}) = \oplus_{p+q=n}C_{G_3}^{p,q}(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{F})
    \end{equation*}
    with vertical and horizontal differentials given by the group and \v{C}ech differentials, denoted $d$ and $\partial$, respectively. The cohomology of the total complex $(C^\bullet_{G_3}(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{F}),D)$ maps to the $G_3$-equivariant cohomology $H^n_{G_3}(X_3,F)$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
The cover $\mathcal{U}$ is a Leray cover for equivariant constant and coherent sheaves. Thus, it is also a Leray cover for $\mathcal{O}^*$, but not necessarily for $\mathcal{M}^*$.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
A framing $f$ is an assignment to each primitive functional $a\in \Lambda$ an oriented basis $f(a)=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ such that $a(x_1)=1$ and $x_2$, $x_3\in \ker(a)$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def: direction vector and modulus}
    Given the ordered pair $(a,b)$ of primitive functionals, we have $\det(a\wedge b\wedge -) = s\gamma \in \Lambda^{\vee}\cong L$, for $s$ a positive integer and $\gamma$ a primitive vector. We define $s$ to be the modulus and $\gamma$ to be the direction vector of the pair $(a,b)$. We will often use the notation $\gamma = (a,b)_L$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def: elliptic Gamma cochain}
    The elliptic Gamma cochain is the following $G_3$-equivariant $1$-cochain valued in $\mathcal{M}^*$:
    \begin{equation*}
        (\Delta^f,\Gamma)\in C^1_{G_3}(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{M}^*) = C^1(G_3,\check{C}^0(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{M}^*)) \oplus C^0(G_3,\check{C}^1(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{M}^*)) 
    \end{equation*}
    The $(1,0)$-cochain $(\Delta^f_a:G_3\rightarrow\mathcal{M}^*(V_a))$ is defined by restriction to the translation subgroup $L$ as:
    \begin{equation*}
        \Delta^f_a((u,g))(w,z) =\Delta^f_a(u)(w,z) = \prod_{k=0}^{a(u)-1}\theta_0\left(\frac{w+kz(x_1)}{z(x_3)},\frac{z(x_2)}{z(x_3)}\right)
    \end{equation*}
    in the case that $a(u)>0$; see \cite{Felder08}[Definition 3.12] for the full generality.
    
    The $(0,1)$-cochain $(\Gamma_{a,b})\in \prod \mathcal{M}^*(V_a\cap V_b)$ is defined as a product of standard elliptic Gamma:
    \begin{equation*}
        \Gamma_{a,b}(w,z) = \prod_{\delta\in F_{a,b}^{\alpha,\beta}}\Gamma\left(\frac{w+z(\delta)}{z(\gamma)},\frac{z(\alpha)}{z(\gamma)},\frac{z(\beta)}{z(\gamma)}\right)
    \end{equation*}
    for the additional choices of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ satisfying $a(\alpha)$, $b(\beta)>0$ and $a(\beta)=b(\alpha)=0$, and index set the following  natural representatives for $L/\langle \alpha,\beta,\gamma\rangle $:
    \begin{equation*}
        F_{a,b}^{\alpha,\beta} = \{\delta\in L/\mathbb{Z}\gamma: 0\leq a(\delta)< a(\alpha), 0\leq b(\delta)< b(\beta)\}.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
The functions are homogeneous in $(w,z)$ and so are well-defined on $V_a$ and $V_a\cap V_b$ respectively. Indeed, $\left(\frac{w}{z(\gamma)},\frac{z(\alpha)}{z(\gamma)},\frac{z(\beta)}{z(\gamma)}\right)$ is a representative for the $\mathbb{C}^*$-equivalence class $[(w,(z(\alpha),z(\beta),z(\gamma)))]$.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
We address the dependence of the cochain $(\Delta^f,\Gamma)$ on the choice of framing $f$ in Section \ref{sec: framing}.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
In \cite{Felder08}[\S 4.3], the $(1,0)$-cochain is defined via $\Delta^{f}_{a}((u,g))(w,z) = \Delta^{f}_{a}(u\circ g^{-1})(w,z)=\Delta^{f}_{a}(gu)(w,z)$. The issue with this definition is that the $(1,1)$ component of $D(\Delta^f,\Gamma)$, namely $\frac{d\Gamma}{\partial \Delta}$, will no longer be $\mathcal{O}^*$-valued, contradicting \cite{Felder08}[Theorem 4.1]. However, this is not too alarming, as the authors appear to use the `correct' definition via restriction in \cite{Felder08}[\S 5.3], suggesting this misstep was a typo.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
Since $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ give a basis of $L\otimes\mathbb{C}$, we can explicitly describe the open:
    \begin{equation*}
        \pi(U_a\cap U_b) = \left\{(z(\alpha):z(\beta):z(\gamma)\in \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{C}): \frac{z(\alpha)}{z(\gamma)}\in \mathbb{L}, \frac{z(\beta)}{z(\gamma)}\in \mathbb{H}\right\}\cong \mathbb{L}\times\mathbb{H}\subset \mathbb{C}^2=\{z(\gamma)\neq 0\}
    \end{equation*}
    In particular, $V_{a}\cap V_b\cong \mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{L}\times\mathbb{H}$ inside the local trivialisation of $\mathcal{O}(1)$ given by $\gamma\in \ker(a)\cap \ker(b)$.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
\label{remark: alpha and beta}
    The choice of a primitive pair $(\alpha,\beta)$ is equivalent to extending $(a,b)$ to a positive $\mathbb{Q}$-basis of $\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ by a primitive functional. Precisely:
    \begin{equation*}
       \{(\alpha,\beta)\in L_{\text{prim}}^2: a(\alpha),b(\beta)>0, a(\beta)=b(\alpha)=0\}\longleftrightarrow \{c\in \Lambda_{\text{prim}}: \det(a\wedge b\wedge c)>0\}
    \end{equation*}
    There are natural notions of minimality on both side. We could pick $\alpha$ and $\beta$ such that $\langle \alpha,\gamma\rangle =\ker(b)$ and $\langle\beta,\gamma\rangle =\ker(b) $. These conditions, together with the positivity constraint, determine $\alpha$ and $\beta$ up to $\mathbb{Z}\gamma$. For the functional $c$, the positivity constraint is equivalent to asking that $c(\gamma)>0$. We could further ask that $c(\gamma)=1$. The notions of minimality are not equivalent: the condition $c(\gamma)=1$ is strictly stronger. In other words, $c(\gamma)=1$ implies that $(\alpha,\beta)$ are chosen minimally, but the converse is false.

    Finally, we note that when $(\alpha,\beta)$ are chosen minimally, the size of the index set is precisely the modulus of the pair, that is $|F_{a,b}^{\alpha,\beta} |=s$.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
The meromorphic function $\Gamma_{a,b}\in \mathcal{M}^*(V_a\cap V_b)$ is independent of the choice of $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
To highlight the role played by $\alpha$ and $\beta$, let us provisionally write $\Gamma_{a,b}^{\alpha,\beta}$. By symmetry, it suffices to focus on the dependence on $\alpha$. The conditions specify $\alpha$ up to positive rescaling and translation by $\mathbb{Z}\gamma$. Since each of the entries of $\Gamma$ are invariant under translation by $\mathbb{Z}$, one can reduce to showing $\Gamma_{a,b}^{\alpha,\beta}$ and $\Gamma_{a,b}^{N\alpha,\beta}$ agree. This then follows directly from the second distribution relation \eqref{eq: second DR}. Alternatively, one can define $\Gamma_{a,b}$ without reference to either $\alpha$ or $\beta$ by describing it as a quotient of infinite products over cones \cite{Felder08}[\S 3.2].
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{theorem: section of gerbe}
    Fix a framing $f$ and consider the $1$-cochain $(\Delta^f,\Gamma)\in C^1_{G_3}(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{M}^*)$. Then $D(\Delta^f,\Gamma)$ lies in $C^2_{G_3}(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{O}^*)$. In particular, it defines a cocycle $[(\Delta^f,\Gamma)]\in H^1_{G_3}(X_3,\mathcal{M}^*/\mathcal{O}^*)$ whose image under the boundary map associated to the long exact sequence associated to:
    \[\begin{tikzcd}
    	0 & {\mathcal{O}^*} & {\mathcal{M}^*} & {\mathcal{M}^*/\mathcal{O}^*} & 0
    	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
    	\arrow[from=1-2, to=1-3]
    	\arrow[from=1-3, to=1-4]
    	\arrow[from=1-4, to=1-5]
    \end{tikzcd}\]
    is $[D(\Delta^f,\Gamma)]\in H^2_{G_3}(X_3,\mathcal{O}^*)$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
In Section \ref{sec: framing}, we prove the cohomology class in $H^1_{G_3}(X_3,\mathcal{M}^*/\mathcal{O}^*)$ is independent of $f$.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
If we took the basis $L=\langle e_1,e_2\rangle$ and expressed $z = (z_1 \hspace{0.2cm} z_2)$ with respect the dual basis, then for the trivialising section $\frac{e_2}{z_2}$, the action above is the same as described in \eqref{eq: homogeneous action} for $(x,\tau)=\left(\frac{w}{z_2},\frac{z_1}{z_2}\right)$ a representative of $\mathbb{C}^*$-equivalence class $(w,z)$.
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lemma: explicit cocycle j}
    We write $j\mathrel{\vcenter{\baselineskip0.5ex \lineskiplimit0pt\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}= d\theta_0: G_2\rightarrow\mathcal{O}^*(\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{H})$. Then, for  
    $l = (u \hspace{0.2cm} v)\in \mathbb{Z}^2$ and $g\in \operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$, such that $g^{-1} = \big(\begin{smallmatrix}
        a&b\\c&d
    \end{smallmatrix}\big)$:
    \begin{equation*}
         j(l)(x,\tau) = \frac{\theta_0(x+u\tau+v,\tau)}{\theta_0(x,\tau)}=e^{2\pi iQ_l(x,\tau)}\quad j(g)(x,\tau) = \frac{\theta_0(\frac{x}{c\tau+d},\frac{a\tau+b}{c\tau+d})}{\theta_0(x,\tau)} = e^{\pi iP_g(x,\tau)}
    \end{equation*}
    for $Q_l(x,\tau)$, $P_g(x,\tau) \in \mathbb{Q}(\tau)[x]$ given by:
    \begin{align*}
        Q_l(x,\tau) &= -ux+\frac{1}{2}u(1+\tau-u\tau ) \\
        P_g(x,\tau) &= x^2\frac{c}{c\tau+d}+x\left(\frac{1}{c\tau+d}-1\right)-\frac{a\tau+b}{6(c\tau+d)}+\frac{\tau}{6}-\frac{1}{6}\Phi(g)
    \end{align*}
    where $\Phi:\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}/12$ is a group morphism defined on generators as $\Phi\left(\big(\begin{smallmatrix}
            1&1\\0&1
        \end{smallmatrix}\big)\right) = 1$, $\Phi\left(\big(\begin{smallmatrix}
            0&1\\-1&0
        \end{smallmatrix}\big)\right) = 3$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The $\mathbb{Z}^2$-cocycle relation follows from $\theta_0(x+1,\tau)=\theta_0(x,\tau)$ and $\theta_0(x+\tau,\tau)=-q_x^{-1}\cdot\theta_0(x,\tau)$. As $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ is generated by $\big(\begin{smallmatrix}
            1&1\\0&1
        \end{smallmatrix}\big)$ and $\big(\begin{smallmatrix}
            0&1\\-1&0
        \end{smallmatrix}\big)$, the general cocycle relation can be deduced from $\theta_0(x,\tau+1)=\theta_0(x,\tau)$ and the identity described in \eqref{eq: cocycle identity}, namely:
    \begin{equation*}
         \theta_0\left(\frac{w}{z_2},\frac{z_1}{z_2}\right)\cdot \theta_0\left(\frac{w}{z_1},\frac{z_2}{z_1}\right) = \exp(-\pi i B_{2,2}(w,z_1,z_2))
    \end{equation*}
    Notice that the left hand side is precisely $j\left(\big(\begin{smallmatrix}
            0&1\\-1&0
        \end{smallmatrix}\big)\right)(x,\tau)=\theta_0(x,\tau)/\theta_0(\frac{x}{-\tau},\frac{1}{-\tau})$, as we have $\theta_0(x,\tau) = \theta_0(-x,-\tau)^{-1}$.
        
    An alternative perspective is provided in \cite{Kato04}, in which the $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$-automorphy factor follows only from the explicit $\mathbb{Z}^2$-cocycle, computation of the divisor of $\theta_0$, and the pushforward relation described in \eqref{eq: general pushforward}. That $\theta_0$ should satisfy an $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$-modularity relation is not surprising: the $\mathbb{Z}^2$-cocycle exhibits $\theta_0$ as a section of a line bundle on the universal elliptic curve over $\mathbb{H}$ whose divisor is the zero section $[\mathcal{O}]$ and pullback by $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ preserves this divisor. This perspective is discussed further in Appendix \ref{appendix: coprime assumption}; for instance, see  Remark \ref{remark: kato perspective}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
For a positive integer $N$, define the $N$-smoothed theta function:
    \begin{equation*}
        \theta_0^N(x,\tau) \mathrel{\vcenter{\baselineskip0.5ex \lineskiplimit0pt\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}= \frac{\theta_0(x,\tau)^N}{\theta_0(Nx,N\tau)}.
    \end{equation*}
    We write $j^N = d\theta_0^N:\mathbb{Z}^2\rtimes\Gamma_0(N)\rightarrow\mathcal{O}^*(\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{H})$ for the smoothed cocycle.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop: j^N trivial}
    For $N$ coprime to $6$, the $N$-smoothed cocycle $j^N$ is trivial. Explicitly, for $l=(u \hspace{0.2cm} v)\in \mathbb{Z}^2$ and $g^{-1}=\big(\begin{smallmatrix}a& b \\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\big)\in\Gamma_0(N)$:
    \begin{equation*}
        \theta_0^N(x+u\tau+v)=\theta_0^N(x,\tau)\quad \theta_0^N\left(\frac{x}{c\tau+d},\frac{a\tau+b}{c\tau+d}\right) = \theta_0^N(x,\tau) .
    \end{equation*}
    In other words, $\theta_0^N$ 
    is a function on the universal elliptic curve over $Y_0(N)$ for $(N,6)=1$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
We can explicitly compute:
    \begin{equation*}
        j^N(l)(x,\tau) = \exp\left(2\pi i\cdot \frac{N-1}{2}u\right)=1\quad\quad j^N(g)(x,\tau) = \frac{j(g)(x,\tau)^N}{j(\alpha g\alpha^{-1})(Nx,N\tau)} =1
    \end{equation*}
    where $\alpha=\big(\begin{smallmatrix}
        N&0\\0&1
    \end{smallmatrix}\big)\in \operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q})$. The assumption $g\in \Gamma_0(N)$ is equivalent to $\alpha g\alpha^{-1}\in \operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$.

    In the appendix, we give a more conceptual proof using the pushforward relation, due to \cite{Kato04}, in the general case $N$ no longer coprime to $6$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
For $a\in \Lambda$ primitive, we write $\gamma= \det(a\wedge - )$ and choose $\alpha\in L$ so that $L=\langle \alpha,\gamma\rangle$ and $a(\alpha)>0$. Then, for $U_a = \{z\in \Lambda\otimes\mathbb{C}-\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{R}:z(\alpha)/z(\gamma)\in \mathbb{H}\}$ and $(w,z)\in V_a =  (\mathbb{C}\times U_a)/\mathbb{C}^*$, we define:
    \begin{equation*}
\theta_a(w,z)=\theta_0\left(\frac{w}{z(\gamma)},\frac{z(\alpha)}{z(\gamma)}\right).
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- remark-16: body_md -->
When $V/L\cong\mathbb{Z}/N$, the geometric notion of smoothing coincides with our earlier notion of $N$-smoothing:
    \begin{equation*}
        \widetilde{\theta}_a(w,z) = \theta_0^N\left(\frac{w}{z(\gamma)},\frac{z(\alpha)}{z(\gamma)}\right).
    \end{equation*}
    This is because the assumption that $a$ extends to a $\mathbb{Z}$-valued functional on $V$ is equivalent to its kernel generating the quotient: in other words, $V/L = \langle \gamma/N\rangle$.

    If we further assume that $N$ is coprime to $6$, then by $\Gamma_0(N)$-invariance this construction is independent of $a$: if $b\in L^{\vee}$ is another primitive functional that extends to $V^{\vee}$, we have $\widetilde{\theta}_a(w,z)=\widetilde{\theta}_b(w,z)$.
<!-- end remark-16 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{corollary: independence of h for IQF}
    Let $(V,L)$ be a pair of rank $2$ lattices with cyclic quotient $V/L\cong \mathbb{Z}/N$ for $(N,6)=1$. Fix $z$ a strictly complex functional and $h$, $h'\in L\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ be two elements both of whose rational span generates $V/L$. Then, for $h\equiv h'$, we have:
    \begin{equation*}
        \widetilde{\theta}_a(z(h),z) =\widetilde{\theta}_{a'}(z(h'),z).
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
By the previous remark and the $\mathbb{Z}^2$-invariance of the $N$-smoothed $\theta_0^N$:
    \begin{equation*}
        \widetilde{\theta}_a(z(h),z) = \widetilde{\theta}_{a'}(z(h),z) =\widetilde{\theta}_{a'}(z(h'),z).
    \end{equation*}
    This proves the independence of $h$ for $\theta_{\mathfrak{a},h}(L)$ by taking $z=\sigma_{\mathbb{C}}$ and $V=\mathfrak{a}^{-1}L$. We observe that for a prime ideal $\mathfrak{a}$, the assumption that $\mathfrak{a}^{-1}L/L$ is a cyclic $\mathbb{Z}$-module is equivalent to $\mathfrak{a}$ having prime norm.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{theorem: KLF}
    Let $K$, $\sigma_{\mathbb{C}}$, $\mathfrak{f}$, $\mathfrak{a}$, $\mathfrak{b}$, and $h$ be as above. Write $L=\mathfrak{f}\mathfrak{b}^{-1}$ and $w_\mathfrak{f}$ for the number of roots of unity in $1+\mathfrak{f}$. Then, the leading term of the smoothed-partial zeta function is given by:
    \begin{equation*}
    \zeta_{\mathfrak{f},\mathfrak{a}}'(\sigma_{\mathfrak{b}},0)=\frac{1}{w_{\mathfrak{f}}} \log|\theta_{\mathfrak{a},h}(L)|^2
\end{equation*}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{example: elliptic units}
    In the example given in \eqref{eq: classical elliptic units}, we considered $K=\mathbb{Q}(i)$, $\mathfrak{f}=(3)$, and $\mathfrak{a}=(2+i)$ of norm $N=5$. Note that $w_{\mathfrak{f}}=1$. Then, for $L=\mathfrak{f}$, we may take $h=4+3i$, $\gamma = 12+9i$ and $\alpha = 3+3i$. 
    \begin{equation*}
        \theta_{\mathfrak{a},h}(\mathfrak{f}) = \theta_0^N\left(\frac{1}{3},\frac{3+3i}{12+9i}\right)\approx 0.232051+ 0.866025i.
    \end{equation*}
    Since the ray class group of conductor $\mathfrak{f}$ has order $2$ and is generated by $\mathfrak{b}=(1+i)$, the conjugate is given by $\theta_{\mathfrak{a},h}(\mathfrak{f}\mathfrak{b}^{-1})$. For this, we take $h=4+3i$, $\gamma = 12+9i$ and $\alpha = \frac{1}{2}(3+3i)$.
    \begin{equation*}
        \theta_{\mathfrak{a},h}(\mathfrak{f}\mathfrak{b}^{-1}) = \theta_0^N\left(\frac{1}{3},\frac{\frac{1}{2}(3+3i)}{12+9i}\right)\approx -3.232051 - 0.866025i.
    \end{equation*}
    This explains the choice of auxiliary data. These elements satisfy $x^2+3x-3i\in \mathbb{Z}[i][x]$ and so are $3$-units in the ray class field $K(\mathfrak{f})$. This concurs with the refinement of Stark's conjecture in the case $S=\{\sigma_{\mathbb{C}},\mathfrak{f}\}$ has size $2$.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
As we stated Stark's Conjecture for $|S|\geq 3$, for which we expect genuine units, let us give an example in this case. So we take $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-2})$, $\mathfrak{f} = (3)= \mathfrak{p}\cdot \overline{\mathfrak{p}} $, and $\mathfrak{a} = (3+\sqrt{-2})$ of norm $N=11$. Again, we have $w_{\mathfrak{f}}=1$. Moreover, since $(3)$ splits, $\mathfrak{f}$ is composite, $|S|=3$ and we expect our $\mathfrak{a}$-smoothed Stark unit to be a genuine unit. As $\mathfrak{b}=(\sqrt{-2})$ generates $\operatorname{Cl}(\mathfrak{f})\cong \frac{(\mathcal{O}/\mathfrak{p})^*\oplus(\mathcal{O}/\overline{\mathfrak{p}})^*}{\mathcal{O}^* \text{ mod }\mathfrak{f}}\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$, we compute:
    \begin{equation*}
        \theta_{\mathfrak{a},h}(\mathfrak{f}) = \theta_0^N\left(\frac{1}{3},\frac{12+3\sqrt{-2}}{39+9\sqrt{-2}}\right)\approx -0.050510 + 0.087486i \quad          \theta_{\mathfrak{a},h}(\mathfrak{f}\mathfrak{b}^{-1}) = \theta_0^N\left(\frac{1}{3},\frac{\frac{1}{2}(12+3\sqrt{-2})}{39+9\sqrt{-2}}\right)\approx-4.949490 - 8.572768i.
    \end{equation*}
    Here, we have taken $h = 13+3\sqrt{-2}$, $\gamma = 39+9\sqrt{-2}$ in both cases, and $\alpha = 12+3\sqrt{-2}$ for the former and $\frac{1}{2}(12+3\sqrt{-2})$ for the latter. We verify that these satisfy $x^2+(5+6\sqrt{-2})x+1\in \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-2}][x]$.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lemma: change of framing}
    The cochain $\psi^{f,f'}$ is $\mathcal{O}^*$-valued and so the $1$-cocycle $(\Delta^f,\Gamma)\in Z^1_{G_3}(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{M}^*/\mathcal{O}^*)$ is independent of $f$. In particular, the cohomology class $[D(\Delta^f,\Gamma)]\in H^2_{G_3}(X_3,\mathcal{O}^*)$ is independent of $f$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Given two framings $f$ and $f'$, we  define the following auxiliary data for each functional $a$. Writing $f(a) = (x_1,x_2,x_3)$ and $f'(a) = (y_1,y_2,y_3)$, we set $l\mathrel{\vcenter{\baselineskip0.5ex \lineskiplimit0pt\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}= y_1-x_1 \in \ker(a)$ and $g\in \operatorname{SL}(\ker(a))$ such that $g\cdot (\begin{smallmatrix}
        y_2 \\y_3
    \end{smallmatrix}) = (\begin{smallmatrix}
        x_2 \\x_3
    \end{smallmatrix})$. Then, we can express the cochain $\psi^{f,f'}$ explicitly in terms of the cocycle $j$ for $\theta_0$:
    \begin{equation*}
        \psi^{f,f'}_{a}(u)(w,z) = \prod_{k=0}^{a(u)-1} j((kl, g))\left(\frac{w+kz(x_1)}{z(x_3)},\frac{z(x_2)}{z(x_3)}\right).
    \end{equation*}
    In particular, $\psi^{f,f'}\in C^1_{G_3}(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{O}^*)$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lemma: a assocaited to (h,z,g)}
    Consider $g\in \operatorname{SL}(\Lambda)$ for which $\chi_g\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$ is irreducible and has negative discriminant and let $z\in\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{C}-\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{R}$ be an eigenfunctional of $g$. Then, for any nonzero element $h\in L\otimes\mathbb{Q}$, there is a unique primitive functional $a\in \Lambda$ such that:
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
        \item $h\in \ker(a,ga)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$,
        \item $z\in U_a$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Since $g$ has no rational eigenvalues, the elements $h,g^{-1}h\in L\otimes \mathbb{Q}$ are linearly independent and therefore, the annihilator $\operatorname{Ann}(\langle h,g^{-1}h\rangle)$ is one-dimensional. This condition specifies the primitive functional $a$ up to a choice of sign; the sign ambiguity corresponds to the two orientations on $\ker(a)$. Since $z(h)/z(g^{-1}h)=z(h)/gz(h)\in\mathbb{C}-\mathbb{R}$, we have exactly one of $z\in U_a$ or $z\in U_{-a}$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
For $g$ and $z$ as in the Lemma above and a nonzero element $h\in L\otimes\mathbb{Q}$, we set:
    \begin{equation*}
        \Phi(h,\langle z \rangle,g) \mathrel{\vcenter{\baselineskip0.5ex \lineskiplimit0pt\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}= \Gamma_{a,ga}(z(h),z)
    \end{equation*}
    where the primitive functional $a$ is uniquely determined by the triple of data.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
This construction yields a well-defined non-zero complex number. That is $\Phi(h,\langle z\rangle,g)\in \mathbb{C}^*$ is independent of the choice of generator of $\langle z\rangle$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Recall that our opens are defined as $V_a = (\mathbb{C}\times U_a)/\mathbb{C}^*$ where $\mathbb{C}^*$-action is diagonal. In particular, $\Gamma_{a,b}(z(u),z)= \Gamma_{a,b}(\lambda z(u),\lambda z)$ for any $\lambda\in \mathbb{C}^*$ and $u\in L\otimes \mathbb{C}$. 
    
    For the non-vanishing of $\Phi(h,\langle z\rangle,g) = \Gamma_{a,ga}(z(h),z)$, we recall that in general $\Gamma_{a,b}(z(-),z)$ is holomorphic and non-vanishing on $\ker(a,b)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ when $z:L\otimes\mathbb{Q}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{Q}$ \cite{Felder08}[Proposition 3.3]. Now observe the following. Firstly, $a$ is chosen so that $h\in \ker(a,ga)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$. Secondly, for $z$ a non-rational eigenfunctional of $g$, the kernel $\ker(z:L\otimes\mathbb{Q}\rightarrow\mathbb{C})$ is a rational vector space of dimension $1$ or $0$ that carries an action of $g$; in particular, since $g$ has no rational eigenvectors, we deduce $z:L\otimes \mathbb{Q}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
Consider a nonzero rational vector $h\in L\otimes\mathbb{Q}$, strictly complex functional $z\in \Lambda\otimes\mathbb{C}-\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{R}$, and automorphism $g\in \operatorname{SL}(\Lambda)$ that has no rational eigenvalues. We call $(h,\langle z \rangle,g)$ an admissible triple for $L$ if:
    \begin{equation*}
        g\cdot \langle z \rangle =\langle z\rangle \quad\quad  g\cdot  h\equiv h \text{ modulo }L.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- remark-17: body_md -->
\label{remark: admissible vector gives admissible triple}
    Observe that an admissible element $h$ for the fractional ideal $L$ in the arithmetic context of \cite{BCG23} gives an admissible triple $(h,\langle \sigma_{\mathbb{C}}\rangle,\varepsilon)$ for $L$. Indeed, $\sigma_{\mathbb{C}}$ is an eigenvector of $\varepsilon$ and the assumption that $h\equiv 1$ modulo $L$ implies $\varepsilon h\equiv h$ modulo $L$; to see this note that $h\in \mathfrak{f}^{-1}L$ and $\varepsilon$ is assumed to lie in $1+\mathfrak{f}$.
<!-- end remark-17 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop: cocycle expression}
    Let $(h,\langle z \rangle,g)$ an admissible triple for $L$. Then, for all $h'\equiv h$ modulo $L$:  
    \begin{equation*}
        \frac{\Phi(h,\langle z \rangle,g)}{\Phi(h',\langle z \rangle,g)}=\psi^{f,g \cdot f}_{b'}(v)(z(h),z)^{-1}\cdot \frac{\phi^{2,0}_a(u,v-u)(z(h),z)}{\phi^{2,0}_{a'}(u,g^{-1}v-u)(gz(h),z) }\cdot \phi^{1,1}_{a,a'}(u)(gz(h),z)\cdot \phi^{1,1}_{b',a}(v)(z(h),z)\cdot \frac{\phi^{0,2}_{a,b,b'}(z(h),z)}{\phi^{0,2}_{a,a',b'}(z(h'),z)}
    \end{equation*}
    where $a$ and $a'$ are the unique primitive functionals associated to $(h,\langle z \rangle,g)$ and $(h',\langle z \rangle,g)$ respectively and we write $b=ga$, $b'=ga'$. Finally, $u$ and $v$ are the elements of $L$ determined by:
    \begin{equation*}
        h'=h+v \hspace{1cm} \text{and}\hspace{1cm} h' = g^{-1}h+u.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The proof will use the three relations coming from the double complex depicted in Figure \ref{figure: double complex} and the assumptions of the Proposition, which we compile here for later use:
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
        \item $z$ is an eigenvector of $g$. \label{item (i)}
        \item $h'\equiv h$ modulo $L$ so that $h'=h+v$ for some $v\in L$.\label{item (ii)}
        \item $gh\equiv h $ modulo $L$ so that $h'=g^{-1}h+u$ for some $u$ in $L$.\label{item (iii)}
    \end{enumerate}
    We immediately deduce the following facts:
    \begin{enumerate}[resume,label=(\roman*)]
        \item $v-u =g^{-1}h-h\in \ker(a)$ since $h\in \ker(a)\cap\ker(ga)$.\label{item (iv)}
        \item $g^{-1}v-u=g^{-1}h'-h'\in \ker(a')$ since $h'\in\ker(a')\cap\ker(ga')$.\label{item (v)}
    \end{enumerate}
    Moreover, recalling the construction of our opens $V_a$ as the quotient of $\mathbb{C}\times U_a$ by a \textit{diagonal} $\mathbb{C}^*$-action, it follows from our assumption that $z$ is an eigenvector of $g$ that $(z(h),g^{-1}z) = (gz(h),z)$.
    
We now begin the proof, starting with our first cocycle relation.

\noindent\textcolor{red}{\tikz[baseline=(char.base)]{
            \node[shape=circle,draw,inner sep=2pt] (char) {1};}} Given a triple of functionals $a,b$ and $c$, we have:
\begin{equation*}
    (\partial\Gamma)_{a,b,c} = \Gamma_{a,b}\Gamma_{b,c}\Gamma_{c,a}=\phi^{0,2}_{a,b,c}.
\end{equation*}
Now consider the decomposition of the figure below into simplices.
\begin{figure}[!htbp]
    \centering
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale = 0.8]
    \tkzDefPoint(0,0){a}  \tkzLabelPoint[below left](a){$a$}
    \tkzDefPoint(3,0){b}  \tkzLabelPoint[below right](b){$b$}
    \tkzDefSquare(a,b)    \tkzGetPoints{b'}{a'}
    \tkzLabelPoint[above left](a'){$a'$} \tkzLabelPoint[above right](b'){$b'$}
    \tkzDrawPolygon(a,b,b',a')
    \tkzDrawSegments[dashed](a,b')
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{Decomposition into simplices}
                          
\end{figure}
The first identity below corresponds to the lower right simplex, the second to the upper left simplex.
\begin{align}\label{eq: Cech cocycle relations 1}
    & (\partial\Gamma)_{a,b,b'}(z(h),z)=\overbrace{\Gamma_{a,b}(z(h),z)}^{\textcolor{red}{\ast}}\Gamma_{b,b'}(z(h),z)\Gamma_{b',a}(z(h),z) =\phi^{0,2}_{a,b,b'}(z(h),z)\\
    & (\partial\Gamma)_{a,a',b'}(z(h'),z)=\Gamma_{a,a'}(z(h'),z)\underbrace{\Gamma_{a',b'}(z(h'),z)}_{\textcolor{red}{\ast}}\Gamma_{b',a}(z(h'),z) =\phi^{0,2}_{a,a',b'}(z(h'),z) \label{eq: Cech cocycle relations 2}
\end{align}
 We are interested in the quotient of the two \textcolor{red}{$\ast$}. Combining equations \eqref{eq: Cech cocycle relations 1} and \eqref{eq: Cech cocycle relations 2} above, we can express the quotient:
\begin{equation}\label{eq: quotients of gamma}
    \frac{\Gamma_{a,b}(z(h),z)}{\Gamma_{a',b'}(z(h'),z)}= \frac{\Gamma_{a,a'}(z(h'),z)}{\Gamma_{b,b'}(z(h),z)}\cdot \frac{\Gamma_{b',a}(z(h'),z)}{\Gamma_{b',a}(z(h),z)}\cdot \frac{\phi^{0,2}_{a,b,b'}(z(h),z)}{\phi^{0,2}_{a,a',b'}(z(h'),z)}.
\end{equation}
There are two observations to make. First, we exploit the readily verified $\operatorname{SL}(\Lambda)$-equivariance of $\Gamma_{a,b}$, explicitly that $\Gamma_{ga,gb}(w,gz)=\Gamma_{a,b}(w,z)$ for $g\in \operatorname{SL}(\Lambda)$; equivalently that $(d\Gamma)_{a,b}(g)(w,z)= 1$.
Together with the assumption \ref{item (i)} that $z$ is an eigenvector for the action of $g$, we deduce the following:
\begin{equation*}
    \Gamma_{g a,g a'}(z(h),z) = \Gamma_{a,a'}(z(h),g^{-1}z)=\Gamma_{a,a'}(gz(h),z).
\end{equation*}
We now use the assumptions \ref{item (ii)} and \ref{item (iii)}, namely that $h'=h+v=g^{-1}h+u$ for $u$, $v\in L$, and recalling also that $g$ acts on $z$ by pullback. Thus, the quotient in \eqref{eq: quotients of gamma} becomes:
\begin{equation*}
    \frac{\Phi(h,\langle z \rangle,g)}{\Phi(h',\langle z \rangle,g)}= \frac{\Gamma_{a,a'}(gz(h)+z(u),z)}{\Gamma_{a,a'}(gz(h),z)}\cdot\frac{\Gamma_{b',a}(z(h)+z(v),z)}{\Gamma_{b',a}(z(h),z)}\cdot \frac{\phi^{0,2}_{a,b,b'}(z(h),z)}{\phi^{0,2}_{a,a',b'}(z(h'),z)}.
\end{equation*}
We observe that both quotients are of the form $(d\Gamma)_{a,b}(u)(w,z) = \Gamma_{a,b}(w+z(u),z)/\Gamma_{a,b}(w,z)$ for $u\in L$. Hence:
\begin{equation}\label{eq: dGamma}
     \frac{\Phi(h,\langle z \rangle,g)}{\Phi(h',\langle z \rangle,g)}=(d\Gamma)_{a,a'} (u)(gz(h),z)\cdot (d\Gamma)_{b',a} (v)(z(h),z)\cdot \frac{\phi^{0,2}_{a,b,b'}(z(h),z)}{\phi^{0,2}_{a,a',b'}(z(h'),z)}.
\end{equation}
We now turn to our second relation.

\noindent \textcolor{red}{\tikz[baseline=(char.base)]{
            \node[shape=circle,draw,inner sep=2pt] (char) {2};}} The second relation $d\Gamma=\phi^{1,1}\cdot \partial\Delta$ allows us to rewrite the expression above in terms of quotients of $\Delta$. Precisely, the relation tells us that:
\begin{equation*}
    (d\Gamma)_{a,b}=\phi^{1,1}_{a,b}\cdot (\partial\Delta)_{a,b}= \phi^{1,1}_{a,b}\cdot \frac{\Delta_a}{\Delta_b}.
\end{equation*}
Thus, we may rewrite the identity in \eqref{eq: dGamma} as:
\begin{align}
    \frac{\Phi(h,\langle z \rangle,g)}{\Phi(h',\langle z \rangle,g)}&=\phi^{1,1}_{a,a'}(u)(gz(h),z)\cdot \frac{\Delta_a(u)(gz(h),z)}{\Delta_{a'}(u)(gz(h),z)}\cdot \phi^{1,1}_{b',a}(v)(z(h),z)\cdot \frac{\Delta_{b'}(v)(z(h),z)}{\Delta_a(v)(z(h),z)}\cdot \frac{\phi^{0,2}_{a,b,b'}(z(h),z)}{\phi^{0,2}_{a,a',b'}(z(h'),z)} \nonumber
    \\ & =\underbrace{\frac{\Delta_a(u)(gz(h),z)}{\Delta_a(v)(z(h),z)}}_{1.}\cdot \underbrace{\frac{\Delta_{b'}(v)(z(h),z)}{\Delta_{a'}(u)(gz(h),z)}}_{2.}\cdot \phi^{1,1}_{a,a'}(u)(gz(h),z)\cdot \phi^{1,1}_{b',a}(v)(z(h),z)\cdot \frac{\phi^{0,2}_{a,b,b'}(z(h),z)}{\phi^{0,2}_{a,a',b'}(z(h'),z)}\label{eq: quotients 1 and 2}
\end{align}
Simplifying the quotients of $\Delta$ in \eqref{eq: quotients 1 and 2} will require us to use our third and final relation.

\noindent \textcolor{red}{\tikz[baseline=(char.base)]{
            \node[shape=circle,draw,inner sep=2pt] (char) {3};}} Our final relation is that $d\Delta=\phi^{2,0}$. In particular, for $u,v\in L$, we have the group cocycle relation:
\begin{equation}\label{eq: delta cocycle relation}
    \phi^{2,0}_{a}(u,v)(w,z)\cdot \Delta_a(u+v)(w,z)=\Delta_a(u)(w,z) \cdot\Delta_a(v)(w+z(u),z).
\end{equation}
The Proposition will follow from the next two claims which resolve each quotient.
\begin{claim}
    $\Delta_a(u)(gz(h),z)/\Delta_a(v)(z(h),z) = \phi^{2,0}_a(u,v-u)(z(h),z)$.
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}
    We use the fact \ref{item (iv)} that $g^{-1}h - h = v-u\in \ker(a)$. Using the cocycle relation, we can write:
    \begin{equation*}
         \phi^{2,0}_a(u,v-u)(w,z)\cdot \Delta_a(u+(v-u))(w,z)=\Delta_a(v-u)(w,z)\cdot \Delta_a(u)(w+z(v-u),z).
    \end{equation*}
    From the definition of $\Delta$, it is apparent that $\Delta_a(v-u)(w,z)=1$ since $v-u\in\ker(a)$. Thus, we have deduced the identity $ \phi^{2,0}_a(u,v-u)(w,z)\cdot \Delta_a(v)(w,z)=\Delta_a(u)(w+z(v-u),z)$ and evaluating at $w = z(h)$ yields:
    \begin{equation*}
        \phi^{2,0}_a(u,v-u)_a(z(h),z)\cdot\Delta_a(v)(z(h),z)=\Delta_a(u)(z(h+v-u),z)=\Delta_a(u)(z(g^{-1}h),z)=\Delta_a(u)(gz(h),z).
    \end{equation*}
    Thus, the first quotient in \eqref{eq: quotients 1 and 2} is equal to $\phi^{2,0}_a(u,v-u)(z(h),z)$.
\end{proof}
\begin{claim}
    $\Delta_{b'}(v)(z(h),z)/\Delta_{a'}(u)(gz(h),z) = (\psi^{f,g\cdot f}_a(v)(z(h),z)\cdot\phi^{2,0}_{a'}(u,g^{-1}v-u)(gz(h),z))^{-1}$.
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}
    From the action of $\operatorname{SL}(\Lambda)$ on the set of framings and the construction of $\psi^{f,f'}$, we deduce the equalities:
    \begin{equation*}
        \Delta^{f}_{g^{-1}a}(g^{-1} v)(w,g^{-1}z)= \Delta^{g\cdot f}_{a}(v)(w,z) = \Delta^f_a(v)(w,z)\cdot\psi^{f,g\cdot f}_a(v)(w,z).
    \end{equation*}
    Applying this with $a'=g^{-1}b'$ and $w=z(h)$ yields:
    \begin{equation*}
        \Delta^f_{a'}(g^{-1}v)(gz(h),z)=\Delta^f_{g^{-1}b'}(g^{-1}v)(z(h),g^{-1}z) = \Delta^f_{b'}(v)(z(h),z)\cdot\psi^{f,g\cdot f}_{b'}(v)(z(h),z).
    \end{equation*}
    Thus, the quotient becomes:
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: delta quotient 1}
        \frac{\Delta_{b'}(v)(z(h),z)}{\Delta_{a'}(u)(gz(h),z)} =  \frac{\Delta_{a'}(g^{-1}v)(gz(h),z)}{\Delta_{a'}(u)(gz(h),z)} \cdot \frac{1}{\psi^{f,g\cdot f}_{b'}(v)(z(h),z)}.
    \end{equation}
    As before, we use the cocycle relation \eqref{eq: delta cocycle relation}, together with fact \ref{item (v)} that $g^{-1}h'-h' = g^{-1}v-u\in\ker(a')$ to deduce:
    \begin{equation*}
        \phi^{2,0}_{a'}(u,g^{-1}v-u)(w,z)\cdot\Delta_{a'}(u+(g^{-1}v-u))(w,z)=\Delta_{a'}(u)(w,z)\cdot\underbrace{\Delta_{a'}(g^{-1}v-u)(w+z(u),z)}_{=1}.
    \end{equation*}
    Evaluating at $w = z(g^{-1}h)=gz(h)$ yields:
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: delta quotient 2}
        \frac{\Delta_{a'}(g^{-1}v)(gz(h),z)}{\Delta_{a'}(u)(gz(h),z)} = \frac{1}{\phi^{2,0}_{a'}(u,g^{-1}v-u)(gz(h),z)}.
    \end{equation}
    Combining equations \eqref{eq: delta quotient 1} and \eqref{eq: delta quotient 2},
     yields the result that the second quotient appearing in \eqref{eq: quotients 1 and 2} is given by:
     \begin{equation*}
         \frac{\Delta_{b'}(v)(z(h),z)}{\Delta_{a'}(u)(gz(h),z)}= \frac{1}{ \psi^{f,g\cdot f}_{b'}(v)(z(h),z)\cdot\phi^{2,0}_{a'}(u,g^{-1}v-u)(gz(h),z)}.
     \end{equation*}
\end{proof}
Combining all the work above finishes the proof of the proposition.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- claim-1: body_md -->
$\Delta_a(u)(gz(h),z)/\Delta_a(v)(z(h),z) = \phi^{2,0}_a(u,v-u)(z(h),z)$.
<!-- end claim-1 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
We use the fact \ref{item (iv)} that $g^{-1}h - h = v-u\in \ker(a)$. Using the cocycle relation, we can write:
    \begin{equation*}
         \phi^{2,0}_a(u,v-u)(w,z)\cdot \Delta_a(u+(v-u))(w,z)=\Delta_a(v-u)(w,z)\cdot \Delta_a(u)(w+z(v-u),z).
    \end{equation*}
    From the definition of $\Delta$, it is apparent that $\Delta_a(v-u)(w,z)=1$ since $v-u\in\ker(a)$. Thus, we have deduced the identity $ \phi^{2,0}_a(u,v-u)(w,z)\cdot \Delta_a(v)(w,z)=\Delta_a(u)(w+z(v-u),z)$ and evaluating at $w = z(h)$ yields:
    \begin{equation*}
        \phi^{2,0}_a(u,v-u)_a(z(h),z)\cdot\Delta_a(v)(z(h),z)=\Delta_a(u)(z(h+v-u),z)=\Delta_a(u)(z(g^{-1}h),z)=\Delta_a(u)(gz(h),z).
    \end{equation*}
    Thus, the first quotient in \eqref{eq: quotients 1 and 2} is equal to $\phi^{2,0}_a(u,v-u)(z(h),z)$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- claim-2: body_md -->
$\Delta_{b'}(v)(z(h),z)/\Delta_{a'}(u)(gz(h),z) = (\psi^{f,g\cdot f}_a(v)(z(h),z)\cdot\phi^{2,0}_{a'}(u,g^{-1}v-u)(gz(h),z))^{-1}$.
<!-- end claim-2 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
From the action of $\operatorname{SL}(\Lambda)$ on the set of framings and the construction of $\psi^{f,f'}$, we deduce the equalities:
    \begin{equation*}
        \Delta^{f}_{g^{-1}a}(g^{-1} v)(w,g^{-1}z)= \Delta^{g\cdot f}_{a}(v)(w,z) = \Delta^f_a(v)(w,z)\cdot\psi^{f,g\cdot f}_a(v)(w,z).
    \end{equation*}
    Applying this with $a'=g^{-1}b'$ and $w=z(h)$ yields:
    \begin{equation*}
        \Delta^f_{a'}(g^{-1}v)(gz(h),z)=\Delta^f_{g^{-1}b'}(g^{-1}v)(z(h),g^{-1}z) = \Delta^f_{b'}(v)(z(h),z)\cdot\psi^{f,g\cdot f}_{b'}(v)(z(h),z).
    \end{equation*}
    Thus, the quotient becomes:
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: delta quotient 1}
        \frac{\Delta_{b'}(v)(z(h),z)}{\Delta_{a'}(u)(gz(h),z)} =  \frac{\Delta_{a'}(g^{-1}v)(gz(h),z)}{\Delta_{a'}(u)(gz(h),z)} \cdot \frac{1}{\psi^{f,g\cdot f}_{b'}(v)(z(h),z)}.
    \end{equation}
    As before, we use the cocycle relation \eqref{eq: delta cocycle relation}, together with fact \ref{item (v)} that $g^{-1}h'-h' = g^{-1}v-u\in\ker(a')$ to deduce:
    \begin{equation*}
        \phi^{2,0}_{a'}(u,g^{-1}v-u)(w,z)\cdot\Delta_{a'}(u+(g^{-1}v-u))(w,z)=\Delta_{a'}(u)(w,z)\cdot\underbrace{\Delta_{a'}(g^{-1}v-u)(w+z(u),z)}_{=1}.
    \end{equation*}
    Evaluating at $w = z(g^{-1}h)=gz(h)$ yields:
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: delta quotient 2}
        \frac{\Delta_{a'}(g^{-1}v)(gz(h),z)}{\Delta_{a'}(u)(gz(h),z)} = \frac{1}{\phi^{2,0}_{a'}(u,g^{-1}v-u)(gz(h),z)}.
    \end{equation}
    Combining equations \eqref{eq: delta quotient 1} and \eqref{eq: delta quotient 2},
     yields the result that the second quotient appearing in \eqref{eq: quotients 1 and 2} is given by:
     \begin{equation*}
         \frac{\Delta_{b'}(v)(z(h),z)}{\Delta_{a'}(u)(gz(h),z)}= \frac{1}{ \psi^{f,g\cdot f}_{b'}(v)(z(h),z)\cdot\phi^{2,0}_{a'}(u,g^{-1}v-u)(gz(h),z)}.
     \end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{corollary: root of unity}
    For $h$ and $h'$ two admissible vectors, the quotient ${\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h}(L)/{\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h'}(L)$ is a root of unity.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The statement that the cocycle $D(\Delta,\Gamma)$ is valued in $\mathcal{O}^*$ can actually be strengthened: the cocycle is actually valued in $\exp(2\pi i \cdot \mathbb{Q}(z(L))[w])$. As discussed in Remark \ref{remark: admissible vector gives admissible triple}, both $(h,\langle\sigma_{\mathbb{C}}\rangle,\varepsilon)$ and $(h',\langle\sigma_{\mathbb{C}}\rangle,\varepsilon)$ are admissible triples, and so:
    \begin{equation*}
        \frac{\Phi(h,\langle \sigma_{\mathbb{C}}\rangle,\varepsilon )}{\Phi(h',\langle \sigma_{\mathbb{C}}\rangle ,\varepsilon )}=\frac{\Gamma_{a,b}(\sigma_{\mathbb{C}}(h),\sigma_{\mathbb{C}};L)}{\Gamma_{a',b'}(\sigma_{\mathbb{C}}(h'),\sigma_{\mathbb{C}};L)}\in \exp(2\pi i \cdot \mathbb{Q}(\sigma_{\mathbb{C}}(L))[\sigma_{\mathbb{C}}(h)]).
    \end{equation*}
    Thus, we conclude that:
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: corolllary root of unity}
         \frac{{\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h}(L)}{{\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h'}(L)} =\frac{\Gamma_{a,b}(h,\mathfrak{a}^{-1}L)}{\Gamma_{a',b'}(h',\mathfrak{a}^{-1}L)}\cdot\frac{\Gamma_{a',b'}(h',L)^{\operatorname{N}(\mathfrak{a})}}{\Gamma_{a,b}(h,L)^{\operatorname{N}(\mathfrak{a})}} \in\exp(2\pi i\cdot  \sigma_{\mathbb{C}}(F)).
    \end{equation}
    The limit formula implies that $|{\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h}(L)|$ is independent of $h$, so that $|{\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h}(L)/{\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h'}(L)|=1$.

    With these two inputs, we are able to deduce the result. We write $x={\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h}(L)/{\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h'}(L)$. Then:
    \begin{equation*}
        \underbrace{\text{Limit formula}}_{|x|=1}\quad + \quad \underbrace{(\ref{eq: corolllary root of unity})}_{\substack{x=\exp(2\pi i \alpha)\\\alpha\in \sigma_{\mathbb{C}}(F)}} \quad \implies \quad \underbrace{\text{Corollary \ref{corollary: root of unity}}}_{\alpha\in \sigma_{\mathbb{C}}(F)\cap\mathbb{R}=\mathbb{Q} \implies x \text{ is a root of unity}} 
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
We have the equality $\mathcal{V} \cap (V^{\vee})_{\text{prim}} = (L^{\vee})_{\text{prim}}\cap (V^{\vee})_{\text{prim}}$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
By applying the snake lemma to:
    \[\begin{tikzcd}
	0 & L & {V} & {V/L} & 0 \\
	\\
	0 & {\mathbb{Z}} & {\mathbb{Z}} & 0 & 0
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow["a", from=1-2, to=3-2]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=1-4]
	\arrow["a", from=1-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow[from=1-4, to=1-5]
	\arrow[from=1-4, to=3-4]
	\arrow[from=3-1, to=3-2]
	\arrow[from=3-2, to=3-3,equal]
	\arrow[from=3-3, to=3-4]
	\arrow[from=3-4, to=3-5]
\end{tikzcd}\]
    we deduce that $a\in\mathcal{V}$ is equivalent to $a(L)=a(V)$, from which the equality follows immediately.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- remark-18: body_md -->
Note that $X=X_3$: for all $\langle z\rangle \in \mathbb{P}(\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{C})-\mathbb{P}(\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{R})$, we have $z\in U_a$ for some $a\in \mathcal{V}$. Writing $L=\oplus \mathbb{Z}e_i$ and $V=\langle e_1,e_2,e_3/N\rangle$, it is clear that the dual functionals $e^1,e^2\in \mathcal{V}$. With respect to this basis, we write $[z]_{\{e^{i}\}}= \begin{pmatrix}
        z_1 & z_2 & z_3
    \end{pmatrix}$. By the assumption $z\notin \mathbb{P}(\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{R})$, it follows that either $z_2/z_3$ or $z_1/z_3\notin\mathbb{R}$. Thus, $z\in U_a$ for at least one of $\pm e^1,\pm e^2$. 

    Despite this, we will continue to use the notation $X$ instead of $X_3$ to indicate that we are using a restricted open cover to compute $G$-equivariant cohomology.
<!-- end remark-18 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
The smoothed elliptic Gamma cochain is the following $G$-equivariant $1$-cochain valued in $\mathcal{M}^*$ for the $G$-invariant open cover $\mathcal{U} = \{V_a\}_{a\in\mathcal{V}}$:
    \begin{equation*}
        (\widetilde{\Delta}^{\underline{f}},\widetilde{\Gamma})\in C^1_{G}(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{M}^*) = C^1(G,\check{C}^0(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{M}^*)) \oplus C^0(G,\check{C}^1(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{M}^*)) 
    \end{equation*}
    where:
    \begin{equation*}
        \widetilde{\Delta}^{\underline{f}}_a(u)(w,z) \mathrel{\vcenter{\baselineskip0.5ex \lineskiplimit0pt\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}= \frac{\Delta^{f_L}_a(u)(w,z;L)^{N}}{\Delta^{f_{V}}_a(u)(w,z;V)} \quad \quad \widetilde{\Gamma}_{a,b}(w,z) \mathrel{\vcenter{\baselineskip0.5ex \lineskiplimit0pt\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}= \frac{\Gamma_{a,b}(w,z;L)^{N}}{\Gamma_{a,b}(w,z;V)}
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
Let $g\in \operatorname{SL}(L^{\vee})\cap \operatorname{SL}(V^{\vee})$, for which $\chi_g\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$ is irreducible and has negative discriminant,  and $z\in\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{C}-\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{R}$ be an eigenfunctional of $g$. Then, for those nonzero elements $h\in L\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ such that associated primitive functional $a$ lies in $\mathcal{V}$, we define:
    \begin{equation*}
        \widetilde{\Phi}(h,\langle z \rangle,g) \mathrel{\vcenter{\baselineskip0.5ex \lineskiplimit0pt\hbox{\scriptsize.}\hbox{\scriptsize.}}}= \widetilde{\Gamma}_{a,ga}(z(h),z).
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
Consider a nonzero rational vector $h\in L\otimes\mathbb{Q}$, strictly complex functional $z\in \Lambda\otimes\mathbb{C}-\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{R}$ and automorphism $g\in \operatorname{SL}(L^{\vee})\cap \operatorname{SL}(V^{\vee})$ that has no rational eigenvalues. We call $(h,\langle z \rangle,g)$ an admissible triple for the pair $(V,L)$ if:
    \begin{equation*}
        g\cdot \langle z \rangle =\langle z\rangle \quad\quad  g\cdot  h\equiv h \text{ modulo }L \quad\quad \langle h\rangle_{\mathbb{Q}} \text{ generates }V/L.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- remark-19: body_md -->
In contrast to the definition for an admissible triple for $L$, for $h'\in h+L$, the triple $(h',\langle z \rangle,g)$ is no longer necessarily admissible for the pair $(V,L)$.
<!-- end remark-19 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop: smoothed cocycle expression}
    Let $(h,\langle z \rangle,g)$ and $(h',\langle z \rangle,g)$ be two admissible triples for the pair $(V,L)$. If $h'\equiv h$ modulo $L$:      
    \begin{equation*}
        \frac{\widetilde{\Phi}(h,\langle z \rangle,g)}{\widetilde{\Phi}(h',\langle z \rangle,g)}=\widetilde{\psi_{b'}^{\underline{f},g \cdot \underline{f}}}(v)(z(h),z)^{-1}\cdot \frac{\widetilde{\phi^{2,0}_a}(u,v-u)(z(h),z)}{\widetilde{\phi^{2,0}_{a'}}(u,g^{-1}v-u)(gz(h),z) }\cdot \widetilde{\phi^{1,1}_{a,a'}}(u)(gz(h),z)\cdot \widetilde{\phi^{1,1}_{b',a}}(v)(z(h),z)\cdot \frac{\widetilde{\phi^{0,2}_{a,b,b'}}(z(h),z)}{\widetilde{\phi^{0,2}_{a,a',b'}}(z(h'),z)}
    \end{equation*}
    where as before $b=ga$, $b'=ga'$, and $u$, $v$ are the elements of $L$ determined by:
    \begin{equation*}
        h'=h+v \hspace{1cm} \text{and}\hspace{1cm} h' = g^{-1}h+u.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Since $g$ acts on $\mathcal{V}$, from our assumption that $a$, $a'\in \mathcal{V}$, it follows that $b$, $b'\in\mathcal{V}$, so that all the smoothed cocycles appearing are well-defined. The result follows immediately from Proposition \ref{prop: cocycle expression} by construction.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- remark-20: body_md -->
\label{remark: geometric / evaluation}
    We quickly discuss the assumptions of Proposition \ref{prop: smoothed cocycle expression}. The assumptions that are carried over from Proposition \ref{prop: cocycle expression} are \emph{geometric} assumptions, in that they imply the triples $(h,\langle z \rangle,g)$ and $(h',\langle z \rangle,g)$ define homologous loops in $X\times_G EG$ as discussed in Section \ref{subsec: geometric}. For the smoothed expression, we only need to impose that $a$, $a'\in \mathcal{V}$. However, we have imposed the stronger condition that 
    $\langle h\rangle_{\mathbb{Q}}$, $\langle h'\rangle_{\mathbb{Q}}$ generate $V/L$; equivalently that $(a,b)$, $ (a',b')\in \mathcal{W}$, for $\mathcal{W}$ defined in \eqref{eq: def of W}. This is an \emph{evaluation} assumption, in the sense that it ensures the functionals are well-placed with respect to the smoothing pair $(V,L)$. To appreciate the necessity of this condition, it is instructive to consider the extremal case of $h\in L$, which we discuss in Appendix \ref{appendix: extremal}.
<!-- end remark-20 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
We call the pair of framings $\underline{f}= (f_L,f_{V})$ a compatible pair if they satisfy the following condition for all $a\in \mathcal{V}$: that $f_L(a)=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ and $f_{V}(a)=(x_1,x_2,\frac{x_3}{N})$.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{theorem: main theorem in main body}
    Let $(h,\langle z \rangle,g)$ and $(h',\langle z \rangle,g)$ be two admissible triples for the pair $(V,L)$. If $h'\equiv h$ modulo $L$ and $(N,6\cdot \operatorname{disc}(\chi_g))=1$, then:
    \begin{equation*}
        \widetilde{\Phi}(h,\langle z \rangle,g) = \widetilde{\Phi}(h',\langle z \rangle,g).
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Since the identity does not depend on the choice of framing, it suffices to prove it for a particular $\underline{f}$. So we pick $\underline{f}$ to be a compatible pair. Propositions \ref{prop: smoothed compatible pairs} and \ref{prop: smoothed phi2,0} imply that the $\widetilde{\psi^{\underline{f},g\cdot\underline{f}}}$ and $\widetilde{\phi^{2,0}}$ terms vanish. Under the assumption that $d(h,h')=3$, Propositions \ref{prop: smoothed phi1,1} and \ref{prop: smoothed phi0,2} imply the remaining contributions from $\widetilde{\phi^{1,1}}$ and $\widetilde{\phi^{0,2}}$ vanish. 

    Finally, by Corollary \ref{corollary: d=3} to Proposition \ref{prop: image of Psi}, if $(N,6\cdot \operatorname{disc}(\chi_g))=1$, for any pair $h$ and $h'$ that form part of an admissible triple, we can always find an $h''$ such that $d(h,h'')=d(h',h'')=3$. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
Let $\mathfrak{f}$, $\sigma_{\mathbb{C}}$, $\mathfrak{b}$, $L$ and $\varepsilon$ be as in the statement of Theorem \ref{theorem: arithmetic theorem in introduction}. Suppose $\mathfrak{a}$ is a prime ideal of prime norm and coprime to $6\operatorname{N}(\mathfrak{f})\cdot \operatorname{disc}(\chi_{\varepsilon})$. Then, for $h$ and $h'$ admissible elements, we have:
    \begin{equation*}
        {\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h}(L) = {\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h'}(L).
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
As discussed in Remark \ref{remark: admissible vector gives admissible triple}, the notion of admissibility in the arithmetic context implies that $(h,\langle \sigma_{\mathbb{C}}\rangle,\varepsilon)$ is an admissible triple for $L$. The second ingredient to admissibility implies that $(h,\langle \sigma_{\mathbb{C}}\rangle,\varepsilon)$ is an admissible triple for the pair $(\mathfrak{a}^{-1}L,L)$. Moreover, for a prime ideal $\mathfrak{a}$, the prime norm assumption is equivalent to $\mathfrak{a}^{-1}L/L$ being cyclic. Then, the result follows from the identity $\widetilde{\Phi}(h,\langle \sigma_{\mathbb{C}}\rangle ,\varepsilon) = {\bf\Gamma}_{\mathfrak{a},h}(L)^{-1}$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- remark-21: body_md -->
The assumption $\mathfrak{a}$ is coprime to $6\operatorname{N}(\mathfrak{f})\cdot \operatorname{disc}(\chi_{\varepsilon})$ excludes a finite set of primes. As $\operatorname{disc}(F/\mathbb{Q})|\operatorname{disc}(\chi_{\varepsilon})$, the condition excludes all primes of $F$ that lie above a rational prime that ramifies in $F/\mathbb{Q}$.
<!-- end remark-21 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop: smoothed compatible pairs}
    Suppose $\underline{f}$ and $\underline{f'}$ are compatible pairs. Then, the smoothed cochain $\widetilde{\psi^{\underline{f},\underline{f'}}}$ is trivial.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
If $\underline{f}$ and $\underline{f'}$ are two compatible pairs, we have $\widetilde{\Delta}^{\underline{f}} =  \widetilde{\Delta}^{\underline{f'}}$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Immediate from \eqref{eq: relate smoothed psi to smoothed delta}.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
For $\underline{f}$ a compatible pair and $g\in \operatorname{SL}(L^{\vee})\cap \operatorname{SL}(V^{\vee})$, we have $\widetilde{\psi^{\underline{f},g\cdot \underline{f}}}$ is trivial.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Recall that $g$ acts on $\mathcal{V}$. In particular, since $\underline{f}$ is compatible, we know that $g\cdot \underline{f}$ is also compatible.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Let $f_L(a)=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ and $f'_L(a)=(y_1,y_2,y_3)$ for some $a\in \mathcal{V}$. It suffices to consider the evaluation of the cochain at $u\in L$ since $\Delta$ is defined via restriction to $L$. Using the identities of 
    \eqref{eq: relate smoothed psi to smoothed delta} and \eqref{eq: smooth delta smooth theta}, we can express:
    \begin{equation*}
     \widetilde{\psi^{\underline{f},\underline{f'}}_a}(u)(w,z)= \prod_{k=0}^{a(u)-1}\theta_0^N\left(\frac{w+kz(y_1)}{z(y_3)},\frac{z(y_2)}{z(y_3)}\right)\cdot \theta_0^N\left(\frac{w+kz(x_1)}{z(x_3)},\frac{z(x_2)}{z(x_3)}\right)^{-1}.
    \end{equation*}
    The result then follows from the two equalities:
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: equalities of smoothed theta}
        \theta_0^N\left(\frac{w+kz(y_1)}{z(y_3)},\frac{z(y_2)}{z(y_3)}\right)=\theta_0^N\left(\frac{w+kz(x_1)}{z(y_3)},\frac{z(y_2)}{z(y_3)}\right)=\theta_0^N\left(\frac{w+kz(x_1)}{z(x_3)},\frac{z(x_2)}{z(x_3)}\right).
    \end{equation}
    For the first equality, we use $y_1 -x_1\in \ker(a)\cap L$ and $\theta_0^N(-,\tau)$ is $\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}\cdot \tau$-periodic. 
    
    Moreover, from the identity $\mathbb{Z}y_2\oplus\mathbb{Z}y_3 = \ker(a)\cap L=\mathbb{Z}x_2\oplus\mathbb{Z}x_3$, we can produce an automorphism $\delta = \big(\begin{smallmatrix} a&b\\c&d  \end{smallmatrix}\big)\in\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ such that $\delta\cdot (\begin{smallmatrix}
        y_2 \\y_3
    \end{smallmatrix}) = (\begin{smallmatrix}
        x_2 \\x_3
    \end{smallmatrix})$. To deduce the second equality in \eqref{eq: equalities of smoothed theta}, it remains to show that $\delta\in \Gamma_0(N)$. This follows from the compatibility of our framings. We know $x_3 = c y_2 +dy_3$ for $c,d\in \mathbb{Z}$ and so $x_3/N = (c y_2 +dy_3)/N\in \ker(a)\cap V = \mathbb{Z}y_2\oplus\mathbb{Z}\frac{y_3}{N}$. In particular, $c/N\in \mathbb{Z}$ and thus $\delta\in \Gamma_0(N)$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop: smoothed phi2,0}
    Suppose $\underline{f}$ is a compatible pair. Then, the smoothed cocycle $\widetilde{\phi^{2,0}}$ is trivial.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Let us first consider $\phi^{2,0}$ restricted to the translation subgroup $L^2\subset G^2$. To begin with, we express the unsmoothed cocycle $\phi^{2,0}(-;L)$ in terms of $\theta_0$. 
    \begin{align}
        \phi^{2,0}_a(u,v)(w,z) &= \frac{\Delta_a(v)(w+z(u),z)\cdot \Delta_a(u)(w,z)}{\Delta_a(u+v)(w,z)} \nonumber \\&= \prod_{k=0}^{a(v)-1}\theta_0\left(\frac{w+z(u)+kz(x_1)}{z(x_3)},\frac{z(x_2)}{z(x_3)}\right)\cdot \theta_0\left(\frac{w+a(u)z(x_1)+kz(x_1)}{z(x_3)},\frac{z(x_2)}{z(x_3)}\right)^{-1}. \label{eq: phi^{2,0} explicit}
    \end{align}
    Since $\underline{f}$ is a compatible pair, we can use \eqref{eq: smooth delta smooth theta} to deduce:
    \begin{equation*}
        \widetilde{\phi^{2,0}_a}(u,v)(w,z) =  \prod_{k=0}^{a(v)-1}\theta_0^N\left(\frac{w+z(u)+kz(x_1)}{z(x_3)},\frac{z(x_2)}{z(x_3)}\right)\cdot \theta_0^N\left(\frac{w+a(u)z(x_1)+kz(x_1)}{z(x_3)},\frac{z(x_2)}{z(x_3)}\right)^{-1}.
    \end{equation*}
    We have $u-a(u)x_1\in \ker(a) = \mathbb{Z}x_2\oplus\mathbb{Z}x_3$ and so by the $\mathbb{Z}^2$-invariance of $\theta_0^N$ each term in the product is $1$.

    Although $\Delta$ is defined by restriction to the translation subgroup, $\phi^{2,0}$ does depend on the lattice automorphism. However, one can verify the following relation:
    \begin{equation*}
        \phi^{2,0}_a((u_1,g_1),(u_2,g_2))(w,z)=\phi^{2,0}_a(u_1,g_1u_2)(w,z)\cdot \psi^{f,g_1\cdot f}_a(g_1u_2)(w+z(u_1),z).
    \end{equation*}
    In particular, the vanishing of $\widetilde{\phi^{2,0}}$ in the general case reduces to the computation above for $L^2$ and Proposition \ref{prop: smoothed compatible pairs} on the vanishing of $\widetilde{\psi^{\underline{f},\underline{f'}}}$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- remark-22: body_md -->
\label{remark: explicit phi2,0}
    We can also verify the proposition by giving an explicit description of $\phi^{2,0}(-;L)$ in terms of exponentials of polynomials. Using the expression in \eqref{eq: phi^{2,0} explicit}, we express $\phi^{2,0}$ in terms of the cocycle $j$ for $\theta_0$:
    \begin{equation*}
        \phi^{2,0}_a(u,v)(w,z) =\prod_{k=0}^{a(v)-1}j(u-a(u)x_1)\left(\frac{w+a(u)z(x_1)+kz(x_1)}{z(x_3)},\frac{z(x_2)}{z(x_3)}\right).
    \end{equation*}
    To use the explicit description of $j$ given in Lemma \ref{lemma: explicit cocycle j}, we first express $u$ and $v$ in terms of the basis specified by the framing $f_L(a) = (x_2,x_2,x_3)$: $u=\sum m_ix_i$ and $v=\sum n_i x_i$. In particular, $u-a(u)x_1 = u-m_1x_1 = m_2x_2+m_3x_3$.
    \begin{align*}
         \phi^{2,0}_a(u,v)(w,z) =\prod_{k=0}^{n_1-1}e^{2\pi i Q_{(m_2 ,m_3)}(\zeta,\tau)} = e^{2\pi i P^{2,0}_a(u,v)(w,z)}
    \end{align*}
    where $P^{2,0}_a(u,v)(w,z) = \sum_{k=0}^{n_1-1}Q_{(m_2 ,m_3)}(\zeta,\tau)$ and $(\zeta,\tau) = \left(\frac{w+a(u)z(x_1)+kz(x_1)}{z(x_3)},\frac{z(x_2)}{z(x_3)}\right)$. Explicitly, we have:
    \begin{equation*}
        P^{2,0}_a(u,v)(w,z) = \frac{n_1m_2}{2z(x_3)}\cdot\left(-2w+z(x_1)(1-n_1-2m_1)+z(x_2)(1-m_2)+z(x_3)\right).
    \end{equation*}
    Then, for $\underline{f}$ a compatible pair, we can explicitly compute:
    \begin{equation*}
        \widetilde{\phi^{2,0}_a}(u,v)(w,z)=e^{2\pi i \left(N\cdot P^{2,0}_a(u,v)(w,z;L)- P^{2,0}_a(u,v)(w,z;V) \right)} = e^{2\pi i\cdot n_1m_2\cdot \frac{N -1}{2}}= 1
    \end{equation*}
    since $N$ is odd. This verifies Proposition \ref{prop: smoothed phi2,0} directly.
<!-- end remark-22 -->
<!-- remark-23: body_md -->
When $(a,b)\in \mathcal{W}$, $\widetilde{\Gamma}_{a,b}$ is a product of $N$-smoothed $\Gamma$-functions, as in \eqref{eq: smoothed elliptic gamma}.
<!-- end remark-23 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop: smoothed phi1,1}
    Suppose $\underline{f}$ is a compatible pair. Then, for $(a,b)\in \mathcal{W}$, the smoothed cocycle $\widetilde{\phi^{1,1}_{a,b}}$ is trivial.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Since $(d\Gamma)_{a,b}(g)$ is trivial for all pairs $a,b$ and $g\in \operatorname{SL}(L^{\vee})$, it follows that $(d\Gamma)_{a,b}((u,g))=(d\Gamma)_{a,b}(u)$. Combining this with $\Delta_a((u,g))= \Delta_a(u)$, we have $\phi^{1,1}_{a,b}((u,g))=\phi^{1,1}_{a,b}(u)$. Thus, it suffices to consider $\widetilde{\phi^{1,1}}$ restricted to $L$ for $u\in L$. We assume for simplicity that $u$ is in the positive cone of $a$ and $b$, with the computations in the other cases proceeding similarly.
    
    The proof will be by reduction to the case of $(a,b)$ of modulus $1$, for the notion of modulus introduced in Definition \ref{def: direction vector and modulus}. If $(a,b)$ has modulus $1$, then we can choose the pair $(\alpha,\beta)$ so that $L=\langle \alpha,\beta,\gamma\rangle $. In particular, we can construct a framing with $f'_L(a) = (\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ and $f'_L(b) = (\beta,\alpha,-\gamma)$. By our assumption that $(a,b)\in\mathcal{W}$, the framing $f_L'$ extends to a compatible pair $\underline{f'}$.

    Using this basis, we write $u=m\alpha +n\beta +l\gamma$, for $m$, $n$, $l\in \mathbb{Z}$ and $m$, $n >0$. We repeatedly apply the difference relation $\Gamma(x+\tau,\tau,\sigma) = \theta_0(x,\sigma)\cdot \Gamma(x,\tau,\sigma)$ to deduce:
    \begin{equation*}
        (d\Gamma)_{a,b}(u)(w,z) = \frac{\Gamma(x+m\tau+n\sigma,\tau,\sigma)}{\Gamma(x,\tau,\sigma)} = \prod_{j=0}^{m-1}\theta_0(x+j\tau+n\sigma,\sigma)\cdot \prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\theta_0(x+k\sigma,\tau)
    \end{equation*}
    where $x = \frac{w}{z(\gamma)}$, $\tau =\frac{z(\alpha)}{z(\gamma)}$ and $\sigma = \frac{z(\beta)}{z(\gamma)}$. From $(a,b)\in \mathcal{W}$, we know $V=\langle \alpha,\beta,\frac{\gamma}{N}\rangle$ and so obtain:
    \begin{align*}
        (d\widetilde{\Gamma})_{a,b}(u)(w,z) &= \prod_{j=0}^{m-1}\theta_0^N(x+j\tau+n\sigma,\sigma)\cdot \prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\theta_0^N(x+k\sigma,\tau)
        \\ & = \prod_{j=0}^{a(u)-1}\theta_0^N\left(\frac{w+jz(\alpha)}{z(\gamma)},\frac{z(\beta)}{z(\gamma)}\right)\cdot \prod_{k=0}^{b(u)-1}\theta_0^N\left(\frac{w+kz(\beta)}{-z(\gamma)},\frac{z(\alpha)}{-z(\gamma)}\right)^{-1} = (\partial\widetilde{\Delta})^{\underline{f'}}_{a,b}(u)(w,z)
    \end{align*}
    where we used $\theta_0(x,\tau) = \theta_0(-x,-\tau)^{-1}$ and the $\mathbb{Z}^2$-invariance of $\theta_0^N$. Since both $\underline{f}$ and $\underline{f'}$ are compatible pairs, it follows from Proposition \ref{prop: smoothed compatible pairs} that $\widetilde{\Delta}^{\underline{f'}} =\widetilde{\Delta}^{\underline{f}}$. Thus, $(d\widetilde{\Gamma})_{a,b} = (\partial\widetilde{\Delta})^{\underline{f}}_{a,b}$ which is equivalent to the vanishing of $\widetilde{\phi^{1,1}_{a,b}}$.

    It remains to reduce to this case for $(a,b)$ of arbitrary modulus. We do so by forming a chain of pairs of reducing modulus, ultimately expressing $\widetilde{\Gamma}_{a,b}$ as a product over modulus $1$ pairs.
    
    To see how this chain is formed, for a pair $(a,b)$ of modulus $s$, we may assume $a=e^1$ and $b=re^1+se^2$ for $0\leq r <s$. But then letting $c=e^2$, we have the coplanar relation $\Gamma_{a,b}  = \Gamma_{a,c}\cdot\Gamma_{c,b}$, where the modulus of $(a,c)$ is $1$ and the modulus of $(c,b)=r <s$. Repeating this process, yields $\Gamma_{a,b}$ as a product of Gamma functions over modulus $1$ pairs. The resulting telescoping product of $(\partial \widetilde{\Delta})^{\underline{f}}_{a_i,a_{i+1}}$ cancels to give the result for $(a,b)$. Notice that every pair in the chain is in $\mathcal{W}$; indeed, $\ker(a,b)=\ker(a_i,a_{i+1})$ since they are coplanar.

    One subtlety is that the above argument only proves the triviality of $\widetilde{\phi^{1,1}}$ in the intersection $\bigcap V_{a_i}\subset V_{a}\cap V_b$ for the functionals $a_i$ appearing in the chain. However, we can always choose the signs of $a_i$ so that the total intersection is an open subset of $V_a \cap V_b$ and then deduce the result by analytic continuation.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
\label{def: d(h,h'}
    Let $(h,\langle z \rangle,g)$ and $(h',\langle z \rangle,g)$ be two admissible triples for the pair $(V,L)$, which uniquely specify the functionals $a$, $a'$, $b=ga$, and $b=ga'$. By admissibility, we know $(a,b)$, $(a',b')\in \mathcal{W}$. We define $d(h,h')\in\{1,2,3\}$ to be the number of pairs in either the upper left or lower right simplex that lie in $\mathcal{W}$:
\begin{figure}[!htbp]
    \centering
    \begin{tikzpicture}[scale = 0.5]
    \tkzDefPoint(0,0){a}  \tkzLabelPoint[below left](a){$a$}
    \tkzDefPoint(3,0){b}  \tkzLabelPoint[below right](b){$b$}
    \tkzDefSquare(a,b)    \tkzGetPoints{b'}{a'}
    \tkzLabelPoint[above left](a'){$a'$} \tkzLabelPoint[above right](b'){$b'$}
    \tkzDrawPolygon(a,b,b',a')
    \tkzDrawSegments[dashed](a,b')
    \label{figure: simplices}
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{figure}
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- remark-24: body_md -->
This number is independent of which simplex we choose because $(a,a')\in\mathcal{W}$ if and only if $(b,b')\in \mathcal{W}$. Moreover, we have $d(h,h')=3\iff (a,a',b')\in\mathcal{Q}\iff (a,b,b')\in\mathcal{Q}$.
<!-- end remark-24 -->
<!-- remark-25: body_md -->
We have dropped both $\langle z\rangle$ and $g$ from the notation as we are only varying $h$. Moreover, for fixed $g$, the invariant $d$ is in fact independent of the choice of eigenline as switching $\langle z\rangle$ to $\langle \bar{z}\rangle$ amounts to changing the sign of the associated functionals $a$ and $a'$ which has no effect on the kernel computation.
<!-- end remark-25 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
Let $(h,\langle z \rangle,g)$ and $(h',\langle z \rangle,g)$ be two admissible triples for the pair $(V,L)$, such that $h'\equiv h$ modulo $L$. If $d(h,h')=3$, then:
     \begin{equation*}
        \frac{\widetilde{\Phi}(h,\langle z \rangle,g)}{\widetilde{\Phi}(h',\langle z \rangle,g)}=\frac{\widetilde{\phi^{0,2}_{a,b,b'}}(z(h),z)}{\widetilde{\phi^{0,2}_{a,a',b'}}(z(h'),z)}.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Both $\widetilde{\Phi}$ and $\widetilde{\phi^{0,2}}$ are independent of a framing by definition and so take $\underline{f}$ to be a compatible pair.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop: smoothed phi0,2}
    Suppose $(a,b,c)\in\mathcal{Q}$. Then the smoothed cocycle $\widetilde{\phi^{0,2}_{a,b,c}}$ is trivial.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop: explicit phi0,2}
    For $(w,z)\in V_{a_1}\cap V_{a_2}\cap V_{a_3}$, the unsmoothed cocycle $\phi^{0,2}$ is given by:
    \begin{equation*}
        \phi^{0,2}_{a_1,a_2,a_3}(w,z)=e^{-\frac{2\pi i }{3!}P^{0,2}_{a_1,a_2,a_3}(w,z)}
    \end{equation*}
    for $P^{0,2}_{a_1,a_2,a_3}(w,z)\in \mathbb{Q}(z(L))[w]$. Explicitly, if $(a_1,a_2,a_3)$ is a positively oriented basis of $\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{Q}$, we have:
    \begin{equation*}
        P^{0,2}_{a_1,a_2,a_3}(w,z) = \sum_{\delta\in F_{a_1,a_2,a_3}(L)} B_{3,3}(w+z(\delta),z(\underline{x})).
    \end{equation*}
