    Here, $x = (x_1,x_2,x_3)$, where $x_1$, $x_2$, and $x_3$ are the direction vectors of the wedges $(a_2,a_3)$, $(a_3,a_1)$, and $(a_1,a_2)$ respectively. Finally, $F_{a_1,a_2,a_3}(L)$ is the following choice of representatives for the quotient $L/\langle x_1,x_2,x_3\rangle$. 
    \begin{equation*}
        F_{a_1,a_2,a_3}(L) = \{\delta\in L: \hspace{0.2cm} 0 \leq a_j(\delta)<a_j(x_j),\hspace{0.2cm} j\in \{1,2,3\} \}.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
This follows directly from the functional identity in \eqref{eq: cocycle identity}:
    \begin{equation*}
        \Gamma\left(\frac{w}{x_3},\frac{x_1}{x_3},\frac{x_2}{x_3}\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{w}{x_1},\frac{x_2}{x_1},\frac{x_3}{x_1}\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{w}{x_2},\frac{x_3}{x_2},\frac{x_1}{x_2}\right) = e^{-\frac{2\pi i}{3!}B_{3,3}(w,\underline{x})}
    \end{equation*} 
    together with the fact that $F_{a_1,a_2,a_3}(L)$ can be used as an index set to define each of $\Gamma_{a_i,a_j}$. Indeed, $F_{a_1,a_2,a_3}(L) $ modulo $\mathbb{Z}x_3$ is precisely $ F_{a_1,a_2}^{x_1,x_2}(L)/\mathbb{Z}x_3$, the index set introduced in Definition \ref{def: elliptic Gamma cochain}. We have the analogous relation for $(a_2,a_3)$ and $(a_3,a_1)$.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- remark-26: body_md -->
If $(a_1,a_2,a_3)$ are linearly dependent, then $\phi^{0,2}_{a_1,a_2,a_3} =1$ so the claim of Proposition \ref{prop: smoothed phi0,2} is immediate. Moreover, from $\Gamma_{a,b}=\Gamma_{b,a}^{-1}$, we deduce $\phi^{0,2}_{a_1,a_2,a_3} = (\phi^{0,2}_{a_1,a_3,a_2})^{-1}$. Thus, it suffices to consider the case $(a_1,a_2,a_3)$ is a positively oriented basis of $\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{Q}$.
<!-- end remark-26 -->
<!-- remark-27: body_md -->
For $\lambda\in \mathbb{C}^*$, if we make the substitution $t\mapsto \lambda t$ in the defining generating series for $B_{n,m}$ in \eqref{eq: exp generating function}, we deduce that the diagonal Bernoulli polynomials satisfy the following homogeneity relation: 
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: Bernoulli homogeneity}
        B_{n,n}(\lambda w,\lambda\underline{x}) = B_{n,n}(w,\underline{x}).
    \end{equation}
<!-- end remark-27 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
\label{def: line and plane}
    A line in $(\mathbb{Z}/N)^3$ will be a submodule isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/N$. A plane in $(\mathbb{Z}/N)^3$ will be a submodule isomorphic to $(\mathbb{Z}/N)^2$.
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop: Bernoulli DR}
    Consider a rank $3$ lattice $U=\bigoplus_{j=1}^3 \mathbb{Z}x_j$. If $P$ is a plane in $\frac{1}{N}U/U\cong (\mathbb{Z}/N)^3$ that trivially intersects each coordinate axis and $(N,6)=1$, then for all $w\in\mathbb{C}$ and complex functionals $z:U\otimes\mathbb{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}$ such that $z(x_j)\neq 0$ we have the following distribution relation:
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: Bernoulli DR}
         N\cdot\sum_{\nu\in P}B_{3,3}(w+z(\nu),z(\underline{x})) \equiv B_{3,3}(Nw,z(\underline{x})) \text{ modulo } 6\mathbb{Z}
    \end{equation}
    where the coset representatives are taken inside of $\{0,\frac{1}{N}\dots,\frac{N-1}{N}\}^3$ and $\underline{x}=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
By writing $\nu=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^3\nu_jx_j$, we can express the left hand side as:
    \begin{align*}
        \sum_{\nu\in P }NB_{3,3}(w+z(\nu),z(\underline{x}))&=\text{Coeff}\left(t^3;3!N\sum_{\nu\in P}e^{(w+z(\nu))t}\prod\frac{t}{e^{z(x_j)t-1}}\right) \\ & =\frac{3!N}{\prod_{j=1}^3z(x_j)}\cdot\text{Coeff}\left(t^3;\sum_{m\geq 0}\frac{w^m}{m!}t^m\sum_{\nu\in P}\prod_{j=1}^3\frac{z(x_j)te^{\frac{\nu_j}{N}z(x_j)t}}{e^{z(x_j)t-1}}\right).
    \end{align*}
    The (single-variable) Bernoulli Polynomials are defined via $\frac{te^{xt}}{e^{t}-1}=\sum_{k\geq 0}B_k(x)\frac{t^k}{k!} $ so that we recognise:
    \begin{equation*}
        \frac{z(x_j)te^{\frac{\nu_j}{N}z(x_jt)}}{e^{z(x_j)t-1}} = \sum_{k\geq 0}B_k\left(\frac{\nu_j}{N}\right)\frac{(z(x_j)t)^k}{k!} .
    \end{equation*}
    Thus, we can explicitly express the coefficient of $t^3$:
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: Bernoulli LHS}
        \sum_{\nu\in P }NB_{3,3}(w+z(\nu),z(\underline{x})) = \frac{3!N}{\prod_{j=1}^3z(x_j)}\sum_{l=0}^3\frac{w^l}{l!}\sum_{k_1+k_2+k_3=3-l}\Psi(k_1,k_2,k_3)
    \end{equation}
    where $\Psi(k_1,k_2,k_3) = \sum_{\nu\in P}\prod_{j=1}^3B_{k_j}\left(\frac{\nu_j}{N}\right)\frac{z(x_j)^{k_j}}{k_j!}$ contributes to the coefficient of $t^{k_1+k_2+k_3}$ in $\sum_{\nu\in P}\prod_{j=1}^3\frac{z(x_j)te^{\frac{\nu_j}{N}z(x_j)t}}{e^{z(x_j)t-1}}$.
    
    For the right hand side, we carry out the same computation, this time using the generating series for the Bernoulli numbers $b_k$ to rewrite:
    \begin{equation*}
        \frac{z(x_j)t}{e^{z(x_j)t}-1}=\sum_{k\geq 0}b_k\frac{(z(x_j)t)^k}{k!}.
    \end{equation*}
    This produces the equality:
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: Bernoulli RHS}
        B_{3,3}(Nw,z(\underline{x})) = \frac{3!}{\prod_{j=1}^3z(x_j)}\sum_{l=0}^3\frac{(Nw)^l}{l!}\sum_{k_1+k_2+k_3=3-l}\psi(k_1,k_2,k_3)
    \end{equation}
    where $\psi(k_1,k_2,k_3) = \prod_{j=1}^3b_{k_j}\frac{z(x_j)^{k_j}}{k_j!}$. Thus, combining \eqref{eq: Bernoulli LHS} and \eqref{eq: Bernoulli RHS}, we can express the difference as:
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{\nu\in P }NB_{3,3}(w+z(\nu),z(\underline{x})) -  B_{3,3}(Nw,z(\underline{x})) = \frac{3!}{\prod_{j=1}^3z(x_j)}\sum_{l=0}^3\frac{w^l}{l!}\sum_{k_1+k_2+k_3=3-l}N\Psi(k_1,k_2,k_3)-N^l\psi(k_1,k_2,k_3).
    \end{equation*}
    Lemma \ref{lemma: vanishing of non constant terms} below shows that the difference $N\Psi(k_1,k_2,k_3)-N^l\psi(k_1,k_2,k_3)$ vanishes in all cases except when $k_1=k_2=k_3=1$. In particular, the only non-zero contribution comes when $l=0$. Thus, the difference is independent of $w$ and can be written as:
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: Bernoulli difference}
         \sum_{\nu\in P }NB_{3,3}(w+z(\nu),z(\underline{x})) -  B_{3,3}(Nw,z(\underline{x})) = \frac{3!}{\prod_{j=1}^3z(x_j)}\left(N\Psi(1,1,1)-\psi(1,1,1)\right)
    \end{equation}
   where we can explicitly write:
   \begin{equation*}
       \Psi(1,1,1) = \sum_{\nu\in P}\prod_{j=1}^3B_1\left(\frac{\nu_j}{N}\right)\cdot z(x_j) 
       \hspace{2.5cm} \psi(1,1,1) = \prod_{j=1}^3b_1\cdot z(x_j).
   \end{equation*}
   We have $B_1(x) = -\frac{1}{2}+x$ and $b_1 = B_1(0)=-\frac{1}{2}$ and thus:
   \begin{equation*}
       N\Psi(1,1,1)-\psi(1,1,1) = \prod_{j=1}^{3}z(x_j)\cdot N\sum_{\nu\in P}\left(-\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{4}\frac{\nu_1+\nu_2+\nu_3}{N}-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\nu_1\nu_2+\nu_2\nu_3+\nu_3\nu_1}{N^2}+\frac{\nu_1\nu_2\nu_3}{N^3}\right) +\frac{1}{8}.
   \end{equation*}
    Since projection onto each coordinate plane induces a bijection with $P$, we explicitly compute:
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{\nu\in P}\nu_1+\nu_2+\nu_3 = 3N\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}m=\frac{3}{2}N^2(N-1)\hspace{1.5cm}  \sum_{\nu\in P}\nu_1\nu_2+\nu_2\nu_3+\nu_3\nu_1 = 3\sum_{m,n=0}^{N-1}mn = \frac{3}{4}N^2(N-1)^2.
    \end{equation*}
    Thus, the difference in \eqref{eq: Bernoulli difference} becomes:
    \begin{equation*}
         \sum_{\nu\in P }NB_{3,3}(w+z(\nu),z(\underline{x})) -  B_{3,3}(Nw,z(\underline{x})) = 3!\left(-\frac{(N-1)^3}{8}+\frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{\nu\in P}\nu_1\nu_2\nu_3\right)
    \end{equation*}
    and is seen to be a rational constant independent of both $w$ and $z$. Since $(N,2)=1$, it follows that $(N-1)^3\in8\mathbb{Z}$ and Lemma \ref{lemma: consant in 6Z} below shows that $\sum_{\nu\in P}v_1v_2v_3\in N^2{\mathbb{Z}}$. In particular, we have shown that:
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{\nu\in P }NB_{3,3}(w+z(\nu),z(\underline{x})) -  B_{3,3}(Nw,z(\underline{x})) = 3!\left(-\frac{(N-1)^3}{8}+\frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{\nu\in P}\nu_1\nu_2\nu_3\right)\in 6 \mathbb{Z}
    \end{equation*}
    is a integer multiple of $6$ independent of $w$ and $z$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lemma: vanishing of non constant terms}
    Let $k_i\geq 0$ integers and set $l=3-(k_1+k_2+k_3)\in\mathbb{Z}$. If one of the $k_i = 0$, then $N\Psi(k_1,k_2,k_3)-N^l\psi(k_1,k_2,k_3)=0$. In particular, among the $(k_1,k_2,k_3)$ with $k_1+k_2+k_3 \leq 3$, the only non-zero contribution is when $k_1 = k_2=k_3=1$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Without loss of generality, suppose that $k_3 = 0$. Thus, $l=3-(k_1+k_2)$. Since the plane $P$ trivially intersects each coordinate axis, projection induces a bijection between $P$ and the $x_1x_2$-coordinate plane. Thus:
    \begin{align*}
        N\Psi(k_1,k_2,k_3)-N^l\psi(k_1,k_2,k_3) & = N\sum_{m,n=0}^{N-1}B_{k_1}\left(\frac{m}{N}\right)\frac{z(x_1)^{k_1}}{k_1!}B_{k_2}\left(\frac{n}{N}\right)\frac{z(x_2)^{k_2}}{k_2!} -N^{l} b_{k_1}\frac{z(x_1)^{k_1}}{k_1!}b_{k_2}\frac{z(x_2)^{k_2}}{k_2!} \\ & =\frac{z(x_1)^{k_1}}{k_1!} \frac{z(x_2)^{k_2}}{k_2!}\cdot\left(N\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}B_{k_1}\left(\frac{m}{N}\right)\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}B_{k_2}\left(\frac{n}{N}\right)-N^{l}b_{k_1}b_{k_2}\right) .
    \end{align*}
    The result then follows from the rank $1$ Distribution Relation for single variable Bernoulli Polynomials:
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{m=0}^{N-1}B_{k_i}\left(\frac{m}{N}\right) = N^{1-{k_i}}b_{k_i}.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lemma: consant in 6Z}
    For $(N,6)=1$ and a plane $P\subset (\mathbb{Z}/N)^3$ that trivially intersects each coordinate axis, the sum of the product of coordinates is divisible by $N^2$:
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{(\nu_1,\nu_2,\nu_3)\in P}\nu_1\nu_2\nu_3\in N^2\mathbb{Z}
    \end{equation*}
    where $\nu_i\in\{0,\dots,N-1\}$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
The key inputs from our assumption that $(N,6)=1$ is that both:
\begin{equation}\label{eq: sum of squares}
    \sum_{m=0}^{N-1}m^2=N\frac{(N-1)(2N-1)}{6}\in N\mathbb{Z} \hspace{1cm}\text{and}\hspace{1cm} \sum_{m=0}^{N-1}m=N\frac{N-1}{2}\in N\mathbb{Z} .
\end{equation}
In particular, we deduce the following useful facts, where, as above, we identify $(\mathbb{Z}/N)^3 = \{0,\dots,N-1\}^3$.
\begin{claim}\label{claim: projection to coord plane}
    For $(N,6)=1$ and a plane $P$ that trivially intersects each coordinate axis, we have $\sum_{\nu\in P}\nu_1\nu_2\in N^2\mathbb{Z}$, where $\nu = (\nu_1,\nu_2,\nu_3)$.
\end{claim}
For the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma: consant in 6Z}, we only need the sum to be in $N\mathbb{Z}$. However, to complete the proof of Proposition \ref{prop: smoothed phi0,2}, we will later require the stronger statement of the claim.
\begin{proof}[Proof of Claim \ref{claim: projection to coord plane}]
    Projection induces a bijection between $P$ and the $x_1x_2$-coordinate plane and so the sum is $\left(\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}m\right)^2\in N^2\mathbb{Z}$.
\end{proof}
\begin{claim}\label{claim: intersection with coord plane}
    For $(N,6)=1$ and a plane $P$ that trivially intersects each coordinate axis, we have $\sum_{\nu\in P,\nu_3=0}\nu_1\nu_2\in N\mathbb{Z}$, where $\nu = (\nu_1,\nu_2,\nu_3)$.
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}[Proof of Claim \ref{claim: intersection with coord plane}]
    By our assumption on $P$, the intersection of $P$ with the $x_1x_2$-coordinate plane is the line $\langle(u_1,u_2,0)\rangle$ for some $u_1$, $u_2\in (\mathbb{Z}/N)^*$. Thus, the sum is congruent to $u_1u_2\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}m^2\equiv 0$ modulo $N$.
\end{proof}
Since $N$ is odd, the claim that $S=\sum_{\nu \in P}\nu_1\nu_2\nu_3\in N^2\mathbb{Z}$ is equivalent to $2S\in N^2\mathbb{Z}$.
\begin{equation*}
    2S = \sum_{\nu_1,\nu_2,\nu_3\neq 0}\nu_1\nu_2\nu_3 + (N-\nu_1)(N-\nu_2)(N-\nu_3) \equiv N\sum_{\nu_1,\nu_2,\nu_3\neq 0}\nu_1\nu_2+\nu_2\nu_3+\nu_3\nu_1\hspace{0.5cm} \text{mod }N^2 
\end{equation*}
By symmetry, it suffices to prove that $\sum_{\nu_1,\nu_2,\nu_3\neq 0}\nu_1\nu_2\in N\mathbb{Z}$. We can write:
\begin{equation*}
    \sum_{\nu_1,\nu_2,\nu_3\neq 0}\nu_1\nu_2 =\sum_{\nu_3\neq 0}\nu_1\nu_2= \sum_{\nu\in P}\nu_1\nu_2- \sum_{\nu_3= 0}\nu_1\nu_2\in N\mathbb{Z}
\end{equation*}
by Claims \ref{claim: projection to coord plane} and \ref{claim: intersection with coord plane} respectively.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- claim-3: body_md -->
\label{claim: projection to coord plane}
    For $(N,6)=1$ and a plane $P$ that trivially intersects each coordinate axis, we have $\sum_{\nu\in P}\nu_1\nu_2\in N^2\mathbb{Z}$, where $\nu = (\nu_1,\nu_2,\nu_3)$.
<!-- end claim-3 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Projection induces a bijection between $P$ and the $x_1x_2$-coordinate plane and so the sum is $\left(\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}m\right)^2\in N^2\mathbb{Z}$.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- claim-4: body_md -->
\label{claim: intersection with coord plane}
    For $(N,6)=1$ and a plane $P$ that trivially intersects each coordinate axis, we have $\sum_{\nu\in P,\nu_3=0}\nu_1\nu_2\in N\mathbb{Z}$, where $\nu = (\nu_1,\nu_2,\nu_3)$.
<!-- end claim-4 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
By our assumption on $P$, the intersection of $P$ with the $x_1x_2$-coordinate plane is the line $\langle(u_1,u_2,0)\rangle$ for some $u_1$, $u_2\in (\mathbb{Z}/N)^*$. Thus, the sum is congruent to $u_1u_2\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}m^2\equiv 0$ modulo $N$.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- remark-28: body_md -->
A near verbatim proof shows the rank $3$ Distribution Relation:
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{j_1,j_2,j_3=0}^{N-1}B_{3,3}\left(w+\frac{\sum j_ix_i}{N},\underline{x}\right) = B_{3,3}(Nw,\underline{x}).
    \end{equation*}
    Notice that this is an \textit{equality} of functions. One can obtain this equality modulo $6\mathbb{Z}$ directly by `taking' the \v{C}ech coboundary of the Distribution Relation:
    \begin{equation*}
       \prod_{j,k,l=0}^{N-1}\Gamma\left(x+\frac{j+k\tau+l\sigma}{N},\tau,\sigma\right)=\Gamma(Nx,\tau,\sigma).
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end remark-28 -->
<!-- remark-29: body_md -->
The notation $F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)$ is not simply meant to mimic that of $F(L)$ and $F(V)$. For our functionals $a_1$, $a_2$, and $a_3$, the set $F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)$ is precisely $F_{a_1,a_2,a_3}(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)$ in the notation of Proposition \ref{prop: explicit phi0,2}.
<!-- end remark-29 -->
<!-- remark-30: body_md -->
It is not immediate that the middle row, the `image sequence', is exact. In general, for a commutative diagram with exact rows:
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: SL digression}
    \begin{tikzcd}
    	0 & A & B & C & 0 \\
    	0 & {A'} & {B'} & {C'} & 0
    	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
    	\arrow[from=1-2, to=1-3]
    	\arrow["a"', from=1-2, to=2-2]
    	\arrow[from=1-3, to=1-4]
    	\arrow["b"', from=1-3, to=2-3]
    	\arrow[from=1-4, to=1-5]
    	\arrow["c"', from=1-4, to=2-4]
    	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
    	\arrow[from=2-2, to=2-3]
    	\arrow[from=2-3, to=2-4]
    	\arrow[from=2-4, to=2-5]
    \end{tikzcd}
    \end{equation}
    it is not always true that the `image sequence`:
    \[\begin{tikzcd}
    	0 & a(A) & b(B) & c(C) & 0 
    	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
    	\arrow[from=1-2, to=1-3]
    	\arrow[from=1-3, to=1-4]
    	\arrow[from=1-4, to=1-5]
    \end{tikzcd}\]
    is exact. In fact, exactness is equivalent to the vanishing of the coboundary map $\partial$ in the Snake Lemma associated to \eqref{eq: SL digression}. This is equivalent to the more easily verified condition $a(A)=b(B)\cap A'$.

    In the case of \eqref{eq: three rows SES}, this means checking that $\pi_{i,j}(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U/U) = \pi_{i,j}(L/U)\cap \left(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}\right)^2$, which is immediate by the surjectivity on the left.
<!-- end remark-30 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop: decomposition after projection}
    For any pair $(i,j)$ and $\delta\in F(L)$, there exists a unique pair $(\nu,\mu)\in F(L\cap{\frac{1}{N}U)}\times F(V)$ such that $\pi_{i,j}(\delta)=\pi_{i,j}(\iota(\nu)+s(\mu))$. That is to say we can decompose $\pi_{i,j}(L/U)$ as:
    \begin{equation*}
        \{(\delta_i,\delta_j):\delta\in F(L)\} = \left\{(\iota(\nu_i)+s(\mu_i),\iota(\nu_j)+s(\mu_j)):\nu\in F\left(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U\right) ,\mu\in F(V)\right\}.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
We can apply the decomposition of \eqref{eq: decomposition of 1/Nf} to $\pi_{i,j}(L/U)$ since $\pi_{i,j}(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U/U) = \left(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}\right)^2$. Essentially, we are simply observing that we can reduce both $\delta_i$ and $\delta_j$ simultaneously modulo $f$. This uniquely specifies an element $\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)$ and then we will have $\pi_{i,j}(\delta-\iota(\nu))\in s(\pi_{i,j}(V/\frac{1}{N}U))$. Since a section $s$ is necessarily injective, this condition uniquely specifies $\mu\in F(V)$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{corollary: sums linear and quadratic}
    We have the identities:
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{\delta\in F(L)}\delta = \sum_{\mu\in F(V)}\sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}\mu+\nu \in V \hspace{1cm} \text{and} \hspace{1cm} \sum_{\delta\in F(L)}\delta^2 = \sum_{\mu\in F(V)}\sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}(\mu+\nu)^2\in \operatorname{Sym}^2(V).
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Since  $x_1x_2x_3\not\in V\oplus\operatorname{Sym}^2(V)$, each term appearing above contains at most two indices. Thus, we can assume $\delta = \iota(\nu)+s(\mu)$. Then, the first identity is given by:
    \begin{align*}
        \sum_{\delta\in F(L)}\delta=\sum_{\delta\in F(L)}\sum_{i=1}^3\frac{\delta_i}{Nf}x_i=&\sum_{\mu\in F(V)}\sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}\sum_{i=1}^3\frac{s(\mu_i)+\iota(\nu_i)}{Nf}x_i
        \\ &=\sum_{\mu\in F(V)}\sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}\sum_{i=1}^3\frac{\mu_i}{f}\frac{x_i}{N}+\frac{\nu_i}{N}x_i=\sum_{\mu\in F(V)}\sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}\mu+\nu
    \end{align*}
    since $\iota(\nu_i)=f\nu_i$ and $s(\mu_i)=\mu_i$ on explicit representatives. The second identity is proved similarly.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{corollary: cubic error term}
We have the following decomposition of $N\cdot P^{0,2}_{a_1,a_2,a_3}(w,z;L)$:
    \begin{align*}
        \sum&_{\delta\in F(L)}B_{3,3}(w+z(\delta),z(\underline{x})) -\sum_{\mu\in F_{a_1,a_2,a_3}(V)} \sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}  B_{3,3}(w+z(\mu)+z(\nu),z(\underline{x}))  \\ & = \frac{1}{z(x_1)z(x_2)z(x_3)}\left(\sum_{\delta\in F(L)}\delta^3-\sum_{\mu\in F(V)}\sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}(\mu+\nu)^3 \right).
    \end{align*}
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
The leading term of $B_{3,3}(w,z(\underline{x}))$ is $\dfrac{w^3}{\prod z(x_j)}$. The result then follows immediately from Corollary \ref{corollary: sums linear and quadratic}.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lemma: sum of a_1a_2(a_3+X)}
For $(N,6)=1$, any $X\in \mathbb{Z}$ and a plane $P\subset(\mathbb{Z}/N)^3$ that trivially intersects each coordinate axis, the following sum is divisible by $N^2$:
\begin{equation*}
    \sum_{(\nu_1,\nu_2,\nu_3)\in P}\nu_1\nu_2[\nu_3+X]_N\in N^2\mathbb{Z}
\end{equation*}
where $\nu_i\in\{0,\dots,N-1\}$.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
We begin by recalling the two claims that were introduced in the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma: consant in 6Z} and which we will require again. Namely, we have for $(N,6)=1$ and a plane $P$ that trivially intersects each coordinate axis:
    \begin{equation*}
         \sum_{\nu\in P}\nu_1\nu_2\in N^2\mathbb{Z}  \hspace{0.5cm}\text{and} \hspace{0.5cm} \sum_{\nu\in P,\nu_3=0}\nu_1\nu_2\in N\mathbb{Z}
    \end{equation*}
    To these two, we add a third claim:
    \begin{claim}\label{claim: sum over level set}
        For $(N,6)=1$, a plane $P$ that trivially intersects each coordinate axis and some $c\in \{0,\dots,N-1\}$ we have $\sum_{\nu\in P,\nu_3=c}\nu_1\nu_2\in N\mathbb{Z}$.
    \end{claim}
    \begin{proof}[Proof of Claim \ref{claim: sum over level set}]
        By our assumption on $P$, the projection $\pi_3:P\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{Z}/N$ surjects. Thus, $\pi_3^{-1}(c)=(y_1,y_2,c) +\langle (u_1,u_2,0)\rangle$ for some $u_1$, $u_2\in (\mathbb{Z}/N)^*$. Therefore, the sum is congruent to:
        \begin{equation*}
            \sum_{\nu\in P,\nu_3=c}\nu_1\nu_2 \equiv  \sum_{m=0}^{N-1}(y_1+mu_1)(y_2+mu_2) \equiv  Ny_1y_2+(u_1y_2+y_1u_2)\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}m+u_1u_2\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}m^2\equiv 0 \text{ mod } N\mathbb{Z}
        \end{equation*}
        by our assumption that $(N,6)=1$.
    \end{proof}
    As in the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma: consant in 6Z}, the claim $S=\sum_{\nu\in P}\nu_1\nu_2[\nu_3+X]_N\in N^2\mathbb{Z}$ is equivalent to $2S\in N^2\mathbb{Z}$.
    \begin{align*}
        2S &= \sum_{\nu_1,\nu_2\neq 0}\nu_1\nu_2[X+\nu_3]_N + (N-\nu_1)(N-\nu_2)[X-\nu_3]_N
        \\
        &\equiv \sum_{\nu_1,\nu_2\neq 0}\nu_1\nu_2([X+\nu_3]_N+[X-\nu_3]_N) - N(\nu_1+\nu_2)[X-\nu_3]_N\hspace{0.5cm} \text{mod }N^2 
    \end{align*}
    Since we have $[X+\nu_3]_N+[X-\nu_3]_N\equiv 2X$ modulo $N$, it follows that $[X+\nu_3]_N+[X-\nu_3]_N=  2X + NC_{\nu_3}$ for some integer $C_{\nu_3}\in\mathbb{Z}$ that depends only on $\nu_3$. Thus, we can write:
    \begin{equation*}
        2S\equiv 2X\sum_{\nu_1,\nu_2\neq 0}\nu_1\nu_2 +N\cdot\left(\sum_{\nu_1,\nu_2\neq 0}\nu_1\nu_2C_{\nu_3}-(\nu_1+\nu_2)[X-\nu_3]_N\right)\hspace{0.5cm} \text{mod }N^2 
    \end{equation*}
    We have seen that the first sum is divisible by $N^2$ and so it remains to show that:
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{\nu_1,\nu_2\neq 0}\nu_1\nu_2C_{\nu_3}+ \nu_3(\nu_1+\nu_2)-X(\nu_1+\nu_2)\overset{?}{\in}N\mathbb{Z}
    \end{equation*}
    Since $C_{\nu_3}$ depends only on $\nu_3$, the sum over the first term can be decomposed into the level sets of $\nu_3$, on which we can use Claim \ref{claim: sum over level set}. That $\sum_{\nu_1,\nu_2\neq 0 }\nu_1\nu_3\in N\mathbb{Z}$ was dealt with in the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma: consant in 6Z}. For the final terms, use $\pi_{1,2}:P\xrightarrow{\sim}(\mathbb{Z}/N)^2$ and so $\sum_{\nu_1,\nu_2\neq 0 }\nu_1=\sum_{\nu_1,\nu_2\neq 0 }\nu_2 = (N-1)\sum_{m=1}^{N-1}m\in N\mathbb{Z}$, which completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- claim-5: body_md -->
\label{claim: sum over level set}
        For $(N,6)=1$, a plane $P$ that trivially intersects each coordinate axis and some $c\in \{0,\dots,N-1\}$ we have $\sum_{\nu\in P,\nu_3=c}\nu_1\nu_2\in N\mathbb{Z}$.
<!-- end claim-5 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
By our assumption on $P$, the projection $\pi_3:P\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{Z}/N$ surjects. Thus, $\pi_3^{-1}(c)=(y_1,y_2,c) +\langle (u_1,u_2,0)\rangle$ for some $u_1$, $u_2\in (\mathbb{Z}/N)^*$. Therefore, the sum is congruent to:
        \begin{equation*}
            \sum_{\nu\in P,\nu_3=c}\nu_1\nu_2 \equiv  \sum_{m=0}^{N-1}(y_1+mu_1)(y_2+mu_2) \equiv  Ny_1y_2+(u_1y_2+y_1u_2)\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}m+u_1u_2\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}m^2\equiv 0 \text{ mod } N\mathbb{Z}
        \end{equation*}
        by our assumption that $(N,6)=1$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop: final error term}
    $\frac{N}{z(x_1)z(x_2)z(x_3)}\left(\sum_{\delta\in F(L)}\delta^3-\sum_{\mu\in F(V)}\sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}(\mu+\nu)^3\right)\in 6\mathbb{Z}$. In particular, we have:
    \begin{equation*}
        N\cdot P^{0,2}_{a_1,a_2,a_3}(w,z;L)  \equiv \sum_{\mu\in F_{a_1,a_2,a_3}(V)} \sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)} N\cdot B_{3,3}(w+z(\mu)+z(\nu),z(\underline{x})) \hspace{0.5cm} \text{mod } 6\mathbb{Z}
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
From Proposition \ref{prop: decomposition after projection}, we can in fact deduce more than Corollary \ref{corollary: cubic error term}. Not only can we decompose the sums over the linear and quadratic terms as in Corollary \ref{corollary: sums linear and quadratic}, but we can do the same for those terms in $\operatorname{Sym}^3{V}$ that contain at most two indices. In other words, the coefficients of $x_i^3$ and $x_i^2x_j$ agree in the two sums $\sum_{\delta\in F(L)}\delta^3$ and $\sum_{\mu\in F(V)}\sum_{\nu\in L\cap\frac{1}{N}U/U}(\mu+\nu)^3$. Thus, the difference is:
    \begin{equation*}
        N\cdot \text{Coeff}\left(x_1x_2x_3;\sum_{\delta\in F(L)}\delta^3-\sum_{\mu\in F(V)}\sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}(\mu+\nu)^3\right)= \frac{3!N}{(Nf)^3}\left(\sum_{\delta\in F(L)}\prod_{i=1}^3\delta_i-\sum_{\mu\in F(V)}\sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}\prod_{i=1}^3(\mu_i+f\nu_i)\right)
    \end{equation*}
    since $\nu=\sum_{i=1}^3\frac{\nu_i}{N}x_i=\sum_{i=1}^3\frac{f\nu_i}{Nf}x_i$. Thus, proving the proposition is equivalent to showing that:
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: difference in cubics}
        \sum_{\delta\in F(L)}\prod_{i=1}^3\delta_i-\sum_{\mu\in F(V)}\sum_{\nu\in L\cap\frac{1}{N}U/U}\prod_{i=1}^3(\mu_i+f\nu_i)\in N^2f^3\mathbb{Z}
    \end{equation}
    We begin by strengthening Proposition \ref{prop: decomposition after projection} so as to explicitly describe $F(L)$ in terms of $F(V)$ and $F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)$. Writing $p:L/U\twoheadrightarrow V/\frac{1}{N}U$, given on representatives in $\left(\mathbb{Z}/Nf\mathbb{Z}\right)^3$ by reduction mod $f$, we have $F(L)=\sqcup_{\mu\in F(V)} p^{-1}(\mu)$. Then the content of Proposition \ref{prop: decomposition after projection} tells us that for each $\mu\in F(V)$, there is a unique $\delta\in F(L)$ such that $\pi_{1,2}(\delta)=s(\pi_{1,2}(\mu))$: that is to say that $\delta\equiv\mu$ mod $f$ and moreover $\delta_1 = \mu_1$, $\delta_2 = \mu_2$. Let us write $D_{\mu}$ for the difference $\frac{1}{f}(\delta_3-\mu_3)$ so that $\delta = \mu + f(0,0,D_{\mu})$. Thus, we can explicitly describe $p^{-1}(\mu)$:
    \begin{equation*}
        p^{-1}(\mu)=\delta+\iota(F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)) = \{(\mu_1+f\nu_1,\mu_2+f\nu_2,\mu_3+f[\nu_3+D_{\mu}]_N): \nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U) \}.
    \end{equation*}
    And so the difference in \eqref{eq: difference in cubics} becomes:
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{\mu\in F(V)}\sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}(\mu_1+f\nu_1)(\mu_2+f\nu_2)\underbrace{(\mu_3+f[\nu_3+D_{\mu}]_N-(\mu_3+f\nu_3))}_{=f([\nu_3+D_{\mu}]_N-\nu_3)}.
    \end{equation*}
    \begin{claim}
    We have the following identities:
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}[\nu_3+D_{\mu}]_N-\nu_3 =\sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}\nu_1\cdot([\nu_3+D_{\mu}]_N-\nu_3)= \sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}\nu_2\cdot([\nu_3+D_{\mu}]_N-\nu_3)=0.
    \end{equation*}
    \end{claim}
    \begin{proof}
        Since $\pi_{i,j}(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U/U)=\left(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}\right)^2$, as long as only two indices appear, we can reindex $\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)$ so that, for example, $\sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}\nu_2\cdot[\nu_3+D_{\mu}]_N=\sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}\nu_2\nu_3$.
    \end{proof}
    Thus, the difference simplifies to:
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: final N^2}
        f^3\cdot \sum_{\mu\in F(V)}\sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}\nu_1\nu_2([\nu_3+D_{\mu}]_N-\nu_3)\overset{?}{\in}N^2f^3\mathbb{Z}
    \end{equation}
    where the $\nu_i\in\{0,\dots,N-1\}$. As we have seen in Lemma \ref{lemma: consant in 6Z}, we know that $\sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}\nu_1\nu_2\nu_3\in N^2\mathbb{Z}$. That $\sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}\nu_1\nu_2[\nu_3+D_{\mu}]_N\in N^2\mathbb{Z}$ is given by Lemma \ref{lemma: sum of a_1a_2(a_3+X)}. This completes the proof of the Proposition.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- claim-6: body_md -->
We have the following identities:
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}[\nu_3+D_{\mu}]_N-\nu_3 =\sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}\nu_1\cdot([\nu_3+D_{\mu}]_N-\nu_3)= \sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}\nu_2\cdot([\nu_3+D_{\mu}]_N-\nu_3)=0.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end claim-6 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Since $\pi_{i,j}(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U/U)=\left(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}\right)^2$, as long as only two indices appear, we can reindex $\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)$ so that, for example, $\sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}\nu_2\cdot[\nu_3+D_{\mu}]_N=\sum_{\nu\in F(L\cap\frac{1}{N}U)}\nu_2\nu_3$.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
By the explicit description of $\phi^{0,2}$ in Proposition \ref{prop: explicit phi0,2}, we know that:
    \begin{equation*}
         \widetilde{\phi^{0,2}_{a,b,c}}(w,z)=e^{-\frac{2\pi i}{3!} \left(N\cdot P^{0,2}_{a,b,c}(w,z;L)- P^{0,2}_{a,b,c}(w,z;V) \right)}.
    \end{equation*}
    Now we have:
    \begin{align*}
        N\cdot P^{0,2}_{a,b,c}(w,z;L) = &\sum_{\delta\in F_{a,b,c}(L)} N\cdot B_{3,3}(w+z(\delta),z(\underline{x})) \\ \equiv & \sum_{\mu\in F_{a,b,c}(V)}N\cdot \sum_{\nu\in L\cap\frac{1}{N}U/U} B_{3,3}(w+z(\mu)+z(\nu),z(\underline{x})) \hspace{0.5cm}\text{ mod } 6\mathbb{Z} \\ \equiv & \sum_{\mu\in F_{a,b,c}(V)} B_{3,3}(N\cdot(w+z(\mu)),z(x)) = P^{0,2}_{a,b,c}(w,z;V) \hspace{0.5cm}\text{ mod } 6\mathbb{Z} 
    \end{align*}
    where the second congruence follows from Proposition \ref{prop: final error term} and the third congruence follows from the Distribution Relation of Proposition \ref{prop: Bernoulli DR}. And so we conclude $\widetilde{\phi^{0,2}_{a,b,c}}(w,z)=1$.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{corollary: proof with d=3}
    Let $(h,\langle z \rangle,g)$ and $(h',\langle z \rangle,g)$ be two admissible triples for the pair $(V,L)$, such that $h'\equiv h$ modulo $L$. If $d(h,h')=3$, then:
    \begin{equation*}
        \widetilde{\Phi}(h,\langle z \rangle,g)=\widetilde{\Phi}(h',\langle z \rangle,g).
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
Consider a morphism $\phi:\mathbb{Z}^n\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}^m$. Then, we have the equivalences:
    \begin{equation*}
        \ker(\phi\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N)=\ker(\phi)\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N\iff \operatorname{Tor}^{\mathbb{Z}}_1(\operatorname{coker}(\phi),\mathbb{Z}/N) = \operatorname{coker}(\phi)[N]=0 \iff \operatorname{im}(\phi\otimes \mathbb{Z}/N) = (\mathbb{Z}/N)^{\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{Z}}(\phi)} 
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Tensor each of the short exact sequences $0\rightarrow\ker(\phi)\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}^n\rightarrow\text{im}(\phi)\rightarrow 0$ and $0\rightarrow\text{im}(\phi)\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}^m\rightarrow\operatorname{coker}(\phi)\rightarrow 0$ with $\mathbb{Z}/N$. Since $\text{im}(\phi)$ is a free $\mathbb{Z}$-module, we then use $\operatorname{Tor}^{\mathbb{Z}}_1(\text{im}(\phi),\mathbb{Z}/N)=0$.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lemma: sufficient condition}
    Let $a$, $b\in V^{\vee}$.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item If $a\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N\in (V/NV)^{\vee}$ is primitive, then $a\in \mathcal{V}$ if and only if $ a\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N|_{L/NV}\in (L/NV)^{\vee} $ is primitive.
        \item The following is a sufficient condition for $(a,b)\in \mathcal{W}$:
        \begin{equation*}
            \langle a\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N|_{L/NV},b\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N|_{L/NV}\rangle = (L/NV)^{\vee}\implies (a,b)\in \mathcal{W}.
        \end{equation*}
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
We have the easily verifiable equivalences for $a\in \mathcal{V}$:
    \begin{equation*}
        V = L+\ker(a)\iff V/NV = L/NV +(\ker(a)+NV)/NV \iff V/NV = L/NV +\ker(a)\otimes \mathbb{Z}/N.
    \end{equation*}
    By the assumption $a\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N\in (V/NV)^{\vee}$ is primitive, we know $\ker(a\otimes\mathbb{Z/N}) = \ker(a)\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N$. In particular,
    \begin{equation*}
        a\in\mathcal{V}\iff V/NV = L/NV +\ker(a\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N)\iff a\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N|_{L/NV} \text{ is primitive}.
    \end{equation*}
    Now consider the second part of the claim. As above, $(a,b)\in \mathcal{W}$ if and only if $V/NV = L/NV +\ker(a,b)\otimes \mathbb{Z}/N$.  The hypothesis implies that $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{Z}}(a,b)=2$. Then, by the Lemma above:
    \begin{equation*}
        \ker((a,b)\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N) =\ker(a,b)\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N \iff \text{im}((a,b)\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N) =  (\mathbb{Z}/N)^2 \iff \langle a\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N,b\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N\rangle \cong (\mathbb{Z}/N)^2.
    \end{equation*}
    Since our hypothesis $\langle a\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N|_{L/NV},b\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N|_{L/NV}\rangle = (L/NV)^{\vee}$ implies $\langle a\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N,b\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N\rangle \cong (\mathbb{Z}/N)^2$, we deduce $\ker((a,b)\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N) =\ker(a,b)\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N $ and then use:
    \begin{align*}
        V/NV = L/NV +\ker((a,b)\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N) &\iff (a,b)\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N:L/NV\xrightarrow{\sim}(\mathbb{Z}/N)^2 \\&\iff \langle a\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N|_{L/NV},b\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N|_{L/NV}\rangle = (L/NV)^{\vee}.
    \end{align*}
    This completes the proof of the Lemma.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- remark-31: body_md -->
By taking the annihilator of these submodules, we can state our conditions in terms of submodules of $L/NV$ rather than the dual. For instance:
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: submodules of dual}
        \langle a\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N|_{L/NV},b\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N|_{L/NV}\rangle = (L/NV)^{\vee}\iff \ker(a\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N|_{L/NV})\cap\ker(b\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N|_{L/NV}) = \{0\}.
    \end{equation}
<!-- end remark-31 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
Suppose that $\langle h\rangle_{\mathbb{Q}}$ generates $V/L$. Then:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item We always have $n\geq 1$. If $N|m$, then $n=1$.
        \item We have $\operatorname{order}_{L\otimes\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}}(h)=\operatorname{order}_{NV\otimes\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}}(h)$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
Both claims follow from the following easily verified fact: if $u\in L$ is a lattice element whose rational span generates $V/L$, then $u\in N^kL\iff u \in N^{k+1}V$ for all $k\geq 0$.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lemma: subsets of R}
    If $N|m$, then $R = h+L$. If $(N,m)=1$, then $R\supset h+N^nL$.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
When $N|m$, we know $n=1$ and so $\frac{m}{N^n}\in \mathbb{Z}$. Thus, in both cases ($h''$ in $h+L$ or $h+N^nL$ respectively) we have $\frac{mh''}{N^n}\equiv \frac{mh}{N^n}\in V/L$.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop: image of Psi}
    Suppose $(N, \operatorname{disc}(\chi_g))=1$. Then, $\Psi(R) = \mathbb{P}(L/NV)$.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{corollary: d=3}
    Suppose $(N, 6\cdot \operatorname{disc}(\chi_g))=1$. Then, for any $h$, $h'\in R$, there exists an $h'' \in R$ such that $d(h,h'')=d(h',h'')=3$.
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
From the Proposition above, we know $|\Psi(R)|=N+1 > 4$ and so given any $4$ lines in $\mathbb{P}(L/NV)$, say arising from $a$, $g^{-1}a$, $a'$, $g^{-1}a'$, we can always find an $h''$ such that $\ker(a''\otimes\mathbb{Z}/N|_{L/NV})$ is distinct from all $4$ of these lines in $\mathbb{P}(L/NV)$. Such an $a''$ will satisfy $a''\sim a$, $g^{-1}a$, $a'$, $g^{-1}a'$ and thus we will have $d(h,h'')=d(h',h'')=3$.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- corollary-11: body_md -->
Suppose $(N, 6\cdot \operatorname{disc}(\chi_g))=1$. Then, for any $h$, $h'\in R$, we have $\widetilde{\Phi}(h,\langle z \rangle,g) = \widetilde{\Phi}(h',\langle z \rangle,g)$.
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lemma: sufficient automorphism}
     Suppose $(N, \operatorname{disc}(\chi_g))=1$. Then, $\psi|_{L/NV}\in \operatorname{Aut}(L/NV)$.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Firstly, since $\det(g)=1$, we note that $\operatorname{disc}(\chi_{g^{-1}}) = \operatorname{disc}(\chi_g) $. Now observe:
    \begin{equation*}
        \chi_{g^{-1}}(x)\equiv \chi_{g^{-1}}(x; V/NV) = \chi_{g^{-1}}(x;V/L)\cdot \chi_{g^{-1}}(x;L/NV)=(x-\lambda)\cdot \chi_{g^{-1}}(x;L/NV)\in(\mathbb{Z}/N)[x].
    \end{equation*}
    By assumption $(N, \operatorname{disc}(\chi_g))=1$, we know $\chi_{g^{-1}}\in (\mathbb{Z}/N)[x]$ cannot have a double root. In particular, $\chi_{g^{-1}}(\lambda;L/NV)\neq 0$ and so $-\lambda+g^{-1}\in \operatorname{Aut}(L/NV)$.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Consider the cases $N$ coprime to $m$ or not separately. First, when $(N,m)=1$, we have $R\supset h + N^nL$. Then:
    \begin{equation*}
        h''\in h+N^nL\implies \frac{mh''}{N^n}\in \frac{mh}{N^n}+mL\longmapsto \frac{mh}{N^n}+\frac{L}{NV}\subset \frac{V}{NV}
    \end{equation*}
    where $(N,m)=1$ to deduce $mL/NV = L/NV$. Under the map $\psi$, this coset surjects onto $L/NV$. In other words, any element of $L/NV$ can be expressed as $\psi(\frac{mh''}{N^n})$ for $h''\in R$. By construction $\psi(\frac{mh''}{N^n})\in \langle h'',g^{-1}h''\rangle_{\mathbb{Q}}$, so that when $\psi(\frac{mh''}{N^n})\neq 0 \in L/NV$, we have $\Psi(h'')  = \langle \psi(\frac{mh''}{N^n})\rangle\in\mathbb{P}(L/NV)$. It follows that $\Psi(R) = \mathbb{P}(L/NV)$. 

    It remains to consider the case $N|m$, for which $n=1$. If $v_N(m)=1$, then the above proof works verbatim as $\frac{m}{N}L/NV = L/NV$. However, when $v_N(m)\geq 2$, we have $\frac{mh''}{N}\equiv \frac{mh}{N}\in V/NV$ for all $h''\in R = h+L$ and so we cannot repeat the proof above. Instead, we shall use the following observation: when $N|m$, we have $\frac{mh}{N}\equiv g^{-1}\frac{mh}{N}\in V/L$, which implies that $\lambda\equiv 1\in (\mathbb{Z}/N)^*$. If we then consider $\psi = - 1 +g^{-1}\in \operatorname{End}(NV\otimes \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$, this restricts to $ -\lambda+g^{-1}\in \operatorname{End}(V/NV)$ and further satisfies $\psi(h)=-h+g^{-1}h\in L/NV$. Then, for $h''\in h+L$, we compute $\psi(h'')\in \psi(h)+\psi(L/NV) = \psi(h)+L/NV = L/NV$. As above, we thus deduce that $\Psi(R) = \mathbb{P}(L/NV)$.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
For $x\in L$, with coordinates $[x]_L= (x_1,x_2,x_3)$, the rational span $\langle x\rangle _{\mathbb{Q}}$ generates $V/L$ if and only if $v_p(Nx_3)\leq v_p(x_1)$, $v_p(x_2)$ for all $p|N$. Assuming this condition, an explicit generator in the rational span is given by $\frac{x}{N\prod p^{v_p(x_3)}}\in V$.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
We know $[x]_V = (x_1,x_2,Nx_3)$. The first step is to produce a primitive vector in $V/NV$ in the rational span. So let $n_p =\min(v_p(x_1),v_p(x_2),v_p(Nx_3))$ for each $p|N$. Then $\frac{x}{\prod p ^{n_p}}\in V/NV$ is primitive so $(\langle x\rangle _{\mathbb{Q}}\cap V)/NV = \langle \frac{x}{\prod p ^{n_p}}\rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}/N$. Reducing this line mod $L$, we obtain the subgroup generated by $\frac{Nx_3}{\prod p^{n_p}}\in V/L\cong \mathbb{Z}/N$. This generates $V/L$ if and only if $(\frac{Nx_3}{\prod p^{n_p}},N)=1$. This is equivalent to $n_p = v_p(Nx_3)$ for all $p|N$, which by the definition of $n_p$, is precisely the condition given in the Lemma above.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- remark-32: body_md -->
Despite the presence of $t$ in the denominator, we have:
    \begin{equation*}
        v_p\left(\frac{m}{Nt}\right) = \begin{cases}
            <0: v_p(m)< v_p(N)
            \\0: v_p(m)= v_p(N)
            \\>0: v_p(m)> v_p(N)
        \end{cases}
    \end{equation*}
    for all $p$. The above is tautologous if $v_p(N) = 0$, so assume $p|N$. The only nontrivial case to check is when $v_p(m)\geq v_p(N)\geq 1$. But when $v_p(m)\geq 1$, we have $v_p(t)=v_p(x_3)=0$.
<!-- end remark-32 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
For $(N,\operatorname{disc}(\chi_g))=1$, we have $\psi|_{L/NV}\in \operatorname{Aut}(L/NV)$.
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
Since $\operatorname{End}(L/NV) = M_2(\mathbb{Z}/N)$, the assertion is equivalent to $\det(\psi) = \chi_{g^{-1}}(\lambda;L/NV)\in (\mathbb{Z}/N)^* \iff \chi_{g^{-1}}(\lambda;L/(pL+NV))\neq 0 \in \mathbb{F}_p$ for all $p|N$. Then, by our previous argument in Lemma \ref{lemma: sufficient automorphism}, we know that a sufficient condition is given by $p\nmid \operatorname{disc}(\chi_g^{-1}(x))=\operatorname{disc}(\chi_g)$ for each $p|N$.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
The constants $c$ and $r$ are the unique positive rational numbers that satisfy:
    \begin{align*}
        c\mathbb{Z}_p=\begin{cases}
            \mathbb{Z}_p&:v_p(m)\geq v_p(N) \\
            \frac{Nt}{m}\mathbb{Z}_p&: v_p(m)< v_p(N)
        \end{cases}\quad\quad\quad 
        r\mathbb{Z}_p  = \begin{cases}
            \mathbb{Z}_p&:v_p(m)\geq v_p(N)\geq 1 \\
            \frac{m}{Nt}\mathbb{Z}_p&: v_p(m)< v_p(N), v_p(N)\neq 0
            \\
            m\mathbb{Z}_p&: v_p(N)=0
        \end{cases}
    \end{align*} 
    for all primes $p$. In particular, $h+cL\subset R$, $rcL/NV = L/NV$, and $\psi(rh)\in L/NV$.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
We omit the $p$-adic valuation verifications and prove the final claims. 

    Since $c\in \mathbb{Z}$, we know that $h+cL\subset h+L$ and therefore, it remains to verify that for each $h''\in h+cL$, its rational span generates the quotient. Indeed, we have:
    \begin{equation*}
        \frac{m}{Nt}h''\in \frac{m}{Nt}h+\frac{m}{Nt}cL\subset \frac{m}{Nt}h+L\longmapsto \frac{m}{Nt}h \in V/L.
    \end{equation*}
    Explicitly, $\frac{m}{Nt}c = \prod_{p|m,p\nmid N}p^{v_p(m)-v_p(N)}\in \mathbb{Z}$.
    
    The second claim follows immediately from $(rc,N)=1$.

    For the final claim, we must show that $\psi(rh)\in L/NV\otimes\mathbb{Z}_p$ for each prime $p$. We will use $\sim$ to denote up to multiplication by $\mathbb{Z}_p^*$. If $v_p(N)=0$, then $rh\sim  mh=0\in L/NV\otimes\mathbb{Z}_p$. Now assume $p|N$. If $v_p(m)<v_p(N)$, then $rh\sim \frac{m}{Nt}h\in V/NV\otimes\mathbb{Z}_p$ and so the result follows from $\psi:V/NV\rightarrow L/NV$. The final case is when $v_p(m)\geq v_p(N)$, so that $rh\sim h\in \frac{1}{m}NV/NV\otimes\mathbb{Z}_p$. By our assumption that $\lambda\equiv 1\in (\mathbb{Z}/p^{v_p(m)})^*$ in this case, it follows that $\psi(rh)\sim -h+g^{-1}h\in L/NV$.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
Suppose $(N,\operatorname{disc}(\chi_g))=1$. Then, for any line $l$ in $L/NV$, there exists an $h''\in R$ such that $(\langle h'',g^{-1}h''\rangle_{\mathbb{Q}}\cap L)/NV = l$. If we further suppose that $(N,6)=1$, then for any pair $h$, $h'\in R$, there exists $h''\in R$ such that $d(h,h'')=d(h',h'')=3$.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
Combining all the above, for $h''\in h+cL$, we know that $-r\lambda h''+ rg^{-1}h''  = \psi(rh'')\in \psi(rh+rcL/NV) = \psi(rh)+\psi(L/NV)=L/NV$. In particular, we can find an $h''\in R$ whose associated line in $L/NV$ is $l$.

    Why do we need $(N,6)=1$? Given four lines in $L/NV$, we need there to exist at least one other line that intersects trivially with each of them. We know that:
    \begin{align*}
        l_1\cap l_2=\{0\}&\iff \det(l_1\wedge l_2)\in (\mathbb{Z}/N)^*\iff \det(l_1\wedge l_2)\in (\mathbb{F}_p)^* \text{ for all }p|N \\ &\iff \text{ the reductions of $l_1$ and $l_2$ are distinct mod $p$ for all $p|N$}.
    \end{align*}
    In particular, if we denote $p_{min}$ to be the smallest prime dividing $N$, then we need $p_{min}+1>4\iff p_{min}\geq 5$. Thus, we require $(N,6)=1$.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{theorem: vanishing cocycle}
    Suppose $(N,6)=1$. Then, the smoothed elliptic Gamma cochain $(\widetilde{\Delta}^{\underline{f}},\widetilde{\Gamma})\in C^1_G(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{M}^*)$ is independent of a compatible pair $\underline{f}$. Moreover, for any compatible pair $\underline{f}$:
    \begin{equation*}
        D(\widetilde{\Delta},\widetilde{\Gamma})= \left(\widetilde{\phi^{2,0}},\widetilde{\phi^{1,1}}\Big\vert_{\mathcal{W}},\widetilde{\phi^{0,2}}\Big\vert_{\mathcal{Q}}\right) =1.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- remark-33: body_md -->
The notation $\widetilde{\phi^{1,1}}\Big\vert_{\mathcal{W}}$ indicates the cochain in $C^{1,1}_G(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{O}^*)$ restricted to double intersections $V_a\cap V_b$ for $(a,b)\in \mathcal{W}$, that is $\widetilde{\phi^{1,1}}\Big\vert_{\mathcal{W}}: G\rightarrow\prod_{(a,b)\in \mathcal{W}}\mathcal{O}^*(V_a\cap V_b)$.
<!-- end remark-33 -->
<!-- corollary-12: body_md -->
If $(a,b,b')$, $(a,a',b')\in\mathcal{Q}$, we have $\Phi_{(h,\langle z\rangle,g)}(\widetilde{\Delta},\widetilde{\Gamma})= \Phi_{(h',\langle z\rangle,g)}(\widetilde{\Delta},\widetilde{\Gamma})$.
<!-- end corollary-12 -->
<!-- corollary-13: body_md -->
If $(N, 6\cdot \text{disc}(\chi_g))=1$, then for any $h$, $h'\in R$, there exists an $h'' \in R$ such that $d(h,h'')=d(h',h'')=3$. In particular, we deduce $\Phi_{(h,\langle z\rangle,g)}(\widetilde{\Delta},\widetilde{\Gamma})= \Phi_{(h',\langle z\rangle,g)}(\widetilde{\Delta},\widetilde{\Gamma})$.
<!-- end corollary-13 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
Smoothing kills the restricted Dixmier-Douady class. Explicitly, we have $\widetilde{\psi}=0$ so that $c(\widetilde{\mathcal{G}})=[\widetilde{\psi}]=0\in  H^3_L(\pi^{-1}\langle z\rangle\cong \mathbb{C},\underline{\mathbb{Z}})$.
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Fix a compatible pair so that $f_L(a)=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ and $f_V(a)=(x_1,x_2,\frac{x_3}{N})$. Then, we compute:
    \begin{equation*}
        \widetilde{\psi}(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=N\cdot \psi(\lambda,\mu,\nu;L)-\psi(\lambda,\mu,\nu;V) =  N\cdot (-n_1m_2l_3) -(-n_1m_2(N\cdot l_3))=0.
    \end{equation*}
    Alternatively, we can see this via our explicit computation of $\widetilde{\phi^{2,0}}$ in Remark \ref{remark: explicit phi2,0} as:
    \begin{equation*}
        \widetilde{\phi^{2,0}_a}(\mu,\nu)(w,z)= e^{2\pi i\cdot n_1m_2\cdot \frac{N -1}{2}}.
    \end{equation*}
    In particular, $\frac{1}{2\pi i}\log(\widetilde{\phi^{2,0}_a})=n_1m_2\frac{N-1}{2}$. Then applying the additive differential we obtain:
    \begin{equation*}
         \widetilde{\psi}(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}d\log(\widetilde{\phi^{2,0}_a})(\lambda,\mu,\nu)= \frac{N-1}{2}\left(n_1m_2+(m_1+n_1)l_2-n_1(l_2+m_2)-m_1l_2\right)=0.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
An admissible triple $(h,\langle z \rangle,g)$ for $L$ defines a loop $(p,(e,x))$ in $X\times_G EG$, where $p=(z(h),z)\in X$ and $x=(gh-h,g)\in G$.
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
To show the $1$-chain $(p,(e,x))$ in $X\times EG$ becomes a $1$-cycle in the quotient $X\times_G EG$, we must show $(p,x)=x\cdot (p,e)$. We compute:
    \begin{equation*}
        x\cdot p = (gh-g,g)\cdot (z(h),z) = (z(h)-gz(gh-h),gz)=(gz(h),gz)=(z(h),z)
    \end{equation*}
    where for the final equality we use that $gz=\lambda z$ for $\lambda\in \mathbb{C}^*$ and that the coordinates on the opens $V_a$ are homogeneous: $V_a = (\mathbb{C}\times U_a)/\mathbb{C}^*$.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
The $1$-cycles associated to $(h,\langle z \rangle,g)$ and $(h',\langle z \rangle,g)$ are homologous when $h\equiv h'$ modulo $L$. In particular, there is a canonical homology class in $H_1(X\times_G EG,\mathbb{Z})$ attached to $(h+L,\langle z \rangle,g)$ where $g\cdot h+L=h+L$ and $g\cdot \langle z\rangle$.
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
The space $X$ retracts onto $\mathbb{P}(\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{C})-\mathbb{P}(\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{R})$, which itself is fibered over the Grassmannian of oriented planes $\operatorname{Gr}_2^+(\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{R})\cong S^2$ with contractible fibers. In particular, $X$ is homotopy equivalent to $S^2$ and $\pi_0(X)=\pi_1(X)=1$. Then, from the long exact sequence on homotopy groups associated to a fiber bundle, projection induces isomorphisms $\pi_1(X\times_G EG)\cong \pi_1(BG)=G$ and $H_1(X\times_G EG,\mathbb{Z})\cong H_1(BG,\mathbb{Z})=G^{ab}$. It therefore suffices to show that the group elements $x$ and $x'$ differ by a commutator in $G$. 
    \begin{equation*}
        x\cdot (x')^{-1}=(gh-h,g)\cdot(gh'-h',g)^{-1} = (gh-h,g)\cdot (g^{-1}h'-h',g^{-1}) = (h'-h-g(h'-h),1)
    \end{equation*}
    By our assumption that $h'\equiv h$ modulo $L$, we have $v=h'-h\in L$. Abusing notation, we write $v$ and $g$ for the group elements $(v,1)$ and $(0,g)$ respectively. Then:
    \begin{equation*}
        x\cdot (x')^{-1} = vgv^{-1}g^{-1}=[v,g]\in [G,G]
    \end{equation*}
    which proves that the loops associated to $(h,\langle z \rangle,g)$ and $(h',\langle z \rangle,g)$ are homologous.

    Alternatively, denoting $H=\operatorname{SL}(L^{\vee})\cap \operatorname{SL}(V^{\vee})$, we use the explicit description of the abelianisation:
    \begin{equation*}
        G^{ab} = (L\rtimes H)^{ab} = (L^{ab})_H\times H^{ab}= (L)_H\times H^{ab}
    \end{equation*}
    Evidently $x\cdot (x')^{-1}=(h'-h-g(h'-h),1)\mapsto (0,1)\in G^{ab}$, as $h'-h-g(h'-h)\in I_HL$ for the augmentation ideal $I_H$.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- remark-34: body_md -->
Recall the identification $C_*(BG) = C_*(EG)_G$: the $G$-equivariant (co)-homology of $EG$ is precisely the (co)-homology of $BG$, which in turn computes the group (co)-homology of $G$. It is standard to make the following change of coordinates when passing from $C_*(EG)$ to the quotient $C_*(BG)$. For instance, on $2$-chains:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=0.2cm,row sep=0.3cm]
	{C_2(EG)} &&& {C_1(EG)} &&& {(g_0,g_1,g_2)} &&& {(g_1,g_2)-(g_0,g_2)+(g_0,g_1)}  \\ \\\\\\
    {C_2(BG)} &&& {C_1(BG)} &&& {[x|y]=[g_0^{-1}g_1|g_1^{-1}g_2] } &&& {[y]-[xy]+[x]=[g_1^{-1}g_2]-[g_0^{-1}g_2]+[g_0^{-1}g_1]}\\
	\arrow["\partial_2",from=1-1, to=1-4]
	\arrow["\pi",from=1-1, to=5-1]
	\arrow["\pi",from=1-4, to=5-4]
	\arrow[maps to, from=1-7, to=1-10]
	\arrow[maps to, from=1-7, to=5-7]
	\arrow[maps to, from=1-10, to=5-10]
	\arrow["\overline{\partial}_2",from=5-1, to=5-4]
	\arrow[maps to, from=5-7, to=5-10]
\end{tikzcd}\]
    This change of coordinates gives a `nicer' formula for $\overline{\partial}$: indeed, $\overline{\partial}_2([x|y]) = [y]-[xy]+[x]$. From this, one easily deduces $H_1(G,\mathbb{Z}) = H_1(BG,\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}G/\langle [y]-[xy]+[x]\rangle = G^{ab} $.
<!-- end remark-34 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
The difference $ (p',[x'])-(p,[x])\in C_1(X\times_G EG)$ is a boundary cycle, that is it lies in the image $\overline{\partial}_2(C_2(X\times_G EG)) = \pi\circ\partial_2(C_2(X\times EG))$. We give an explicit preimage below.
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
As before, we abuse notation and write $v$ for the element $(h'-h,1)\in G$. One easily verifies $v^{-1}\cdot x=(gh-h',g)$ and $v^{-1}\cdot p=p'$. Then:
     \begin{align*}
        &\pi\circ\partial_2(((p,(e,(gh'-h,g),x))-(p',(e,-v,x'))) \\&=  (p',[-v])-(p,[x])+(p,[(gh'-h,g])- \big((p,[(gh'-h,g)])-(p',[x'])+(p',[-v])\big) \\ & = (p',[x'])- (p,[x]).
    \end{align*}
    This explicitly verifies the identity $(p',[x'])=(p,[x])\in H_1(X\times_G EG,\mathbb{Z})$.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
Consider an admissible triple $(h,\langle z \rangle,g)$ for $L$. Then, we define a group morphism $\Phi_{(h,\langle z\rangle,g)}:C^1_G(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{M}^*)\rightarrow \mathbb{C}^{*}$ via:
    \begin{equation*}
        (\phi^{1,0},\phi^{0,1})\mapsto \phi^{1,0}_a(x^{-1})(p)\cdot \phi^{0,1}_{a,ga}(p)
    \end{equation*}
    where $p=(z(h),z)$ and $x=(gh-h,g)$.
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
We have $\Phi_{(h,\langle z\rangle,g)}(\widetilde{\Delta},\widetilde{\Gamma}) = \widetilde{\Gamma}_{a,ga}(z(h),z)$. In particular, this evaluation map extends our previous procedure.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
It suffices to show that $\widetilde{\Delta}_a(x^{-1})(p)=1$. We have $x^{-1}=(g^{-1}h-h,g^{-1})$ and by definition $\widetilde{\Delta}_a((g^{-1}h-h,g^{-1}))=\widetilde{\Delta}_a(g^{-1}h-h)=1\in\mathcal{M}^*(V_a)$ as $g^{-1}h-h\in \ker(a)$.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- proposition-18: body_md -->
$\Phi_{(h,\langle z\rangle,g)}:H^1_G(X,\mathcal{M}^*)\rightarrow \mathbb{C}^*$ is well-defined.
<!-- end proposition-18 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
We must show that $\Phi_{(h,\langle z\rangle,g)}$ is trivial on boundaries $B^1_G(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{M}^*)=D(C^{0}_G(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{M}^*))$. To that end, let $f\in C^{0}_G(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{M}^*)=\prod_{a\in \mathcal{V}}\mathcal{M}^*(V_a)$. Then:
    \begin{align*}
        \Phi_{(h,\langle z\rangle,g)}(Df)&=(df)_a(x^{-1})(p)\cdot (\partial f)_{a,ga}(p) \\& = \frac{f_{ga}(x\cdot p)}{f_a(p)}\cdot \frac{f_a(p)}{f_{ga}(p)} = 1
    \end{align*}
    since $x\cdot p = p$. Notice that the numerator for the left quotient is $f_{ga}(x\cdot p)$ not $f_a(x\cdot p)$ as $x\cdot p = (gz(h),gz) \in V_{ga}$.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- proposition-19: body_md -->
Suppose $h\equiv h'$ modulo $L$. Then, we have:
    \begin{equation*}
        \frac{\Phi_{(h,\langle z\rangle,g)}}{\Phi_{(h',\langle z\rangle,g)}}\left(\phi^{1,0},\phi^{0,1}\right) = \text{ expression in } D(\phi^{1,0},\phi^{0,1})
    \end{equation*}
    for some expression that is given explicitly below. Thus, if $(\phi^{1,0},\phi^{0,1})\in Z^1_G(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{M}^*)$, we have:
    \begin{equation*}
        \Phi_{(h,\langle z\rangle,g)}(\phi^{1,0},\phi^{0,1}) =\Phi_{(h',\langle z\rangle,g)}(\phi^{1,0},\phi^{0,1}) 
    \end{equation*}
    and in particular, $\Phi_{(h,\langle z\rangle,g)}=\Phi_{(h',\langle z\rangle,g)}: H^1_G(X,\mathcal{M}^*)\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^*$.
<!-- end proposition-19 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
We need to compute:
\begin{equation}\label{eq: initial quotient}
    \frac{\Phi_{(h,\langle z\rangle,g)}}{\Phi_{(h',\langle z\rangle,g)}}\left(\phi^{1,0},\phi^{0,1}\right) = \frac{\phi^{1,0}_a(x^{-1})(p)\cdot \phi^{0,1}_{a,ga}(p) }{\phi^{1,0}_{a'}(x'^{-1})(p')\cdot \phi^{0,1}_{a',ga'}(p')}.
\end{equation}
As in the proof for the cocycle expression for $(\Delta^f,\Gamma)$, we use the relations:
\begin{align*}
    & (\partial\phi^{0,1})_{a,ga,ga'}(p)=\overbrace{\phi^{0,1}_{a,ga}(p)}^{\textcolor{red}{\ast}}\phi^{0,1}_{ga,ga'}(p)\phi^{0,1}_{ga',a}(p) =\phi^{0,2}_{a,ga,ga'}(p)\\
    & (\partial\phi^{0,1})_{a,a',ga'}(p')=\phi^{0,1}_{a,a'}(p')\underbrace{\phi^{0,1}_{a',ga'}(p')}_{\textcolor{red}{\ast}}\phi^{0,1}_{ga',a}(p') =\phi^{0,2}_{a,a',ga'}(p') 
\end{align*}
to rewrite:
\begin{equation*}
    \frac{\phi^{0,1}_{a,ga}(p) }{ \phi^{0,1}_{a',ga'}(p') } = \frac{\phi^{0,2}_{a,ga,ga'}(p)}{\phi^{0,2}_{a,a',ga'}(p') }\cdot\frac{\phi^{0,1}_{a,a'}(p')}{\phi^{0,1}_{ga,ga'}(p)}\cdot \frac{\phi^{0,1}_{ga',a}(p') }{\phi^{0,1}_{ga',a}(p) }.
\end{equation*}
By definition, $(d\phi^{0,1})_{a,b}(v)(w,z) = \phi^{0,1}_{a,b}(w+z(v),z)/\phi^{0,1}_{a,b}(w,z)$, so setting $v = h'-h$ as usual, we have ensures $p'=(z(h'),z) = (z(h)+z(v),z)$ and thus:
\begin{equation}\label{eq: second quotient}
    \frac{\phi^{0,1}_{ga',a}(p') }{\phi^{0,1}_{ga',a}(p) } = (d\phi^{0,1})_{ga',a}(v)(p) = \phi^{1,1}_{ga',a}(v)(p)\cdot (\partial\phi^{1,0})_{ga',a}(v)(p)
\end{equation}
by definition of the differential $D(\phi^{1,0},\phi^{0,1})$. 

Moreover, we have $(gh'-h,g)\cdot p' = (z(h')-gz(gh'-h),gz)=(z(gh')-z(gh'-h),z)=p$. And thus:
\begin{align}
    \frac{\phi^{0,1}_{ga,ga'}(p)}{\phi^{0,1}_{a,a'}(p')} = \frac{\phi^{0,1}_{ga,ga'}((gh'-h,g)\cdot p')}{\phi^{0,1}_{a,a'}(p')} &= (d\phi^{0,1})_{a,a'}((gh'-h,g)^{-1})(p') \notag \\&= \phi^{1,1}_{a,a'}((g^{-1}h-h',g^{-1}))(p') \cdot (\partial \phi^{1,0})_{a,a'}((g^{-1}h-h',g^{-1}))(p') \label{eq: first quotient}
\end{align}
where we use $(gh'-h,g)^{-1}=(g^{-1}h-h',g^{-1})$. Now combining equations \eqref{eq: second quotient} and \eqref{eq: first quotient}, we can rewrite \eqref{eq: initial quotient}:
\begin{align*}
    \frac{\Phi_{(h,\langle z\rangle,g)}}{\Phi_{(h',\langle z\rangle,g)}}\left(\phi^{1,0},\phi^{0,1}\right) = &\frac{\phi^{1,0}_a(x^{-1})(p)}{\phi^{1,0}_{a'}(x'^{-1})(p')}\cdot \frac{\phi^{1,0}_{a'}((g^{-1}h-h',g^{-1}))(p')}{\phi^{1,0}_{a}((g^{-1}h-h',g^{-1}))(p')}\cdot \frac{\phi^{1,0}_{ga'}(v)(p)}{\phi^{1,0}_{a}(v)(p)} \\&\cdot \phi^{1,1}_{a,a'}((g^{-1}h-h',g^{-1}))(p')^{-1}\cdot \phi^{1,1}_{ga',a}(v)(p)\cdot \frac{\phi^{0,2}_{a,ga,ga'}(p)}{\phi^{0,2}_{a,a',ga'}(p')}.
\end{align*}
Now we use the final relation:
\begin{equation*}
    \phi^{2,0}_a(x_1,x_2)(q) =\frac{ \phi^{1,0}_a(x_1)(q)\cdot\phi^{1,0}_a(x_2)(x_1^{-1}\cdot q)}{\phi^{1,0}_a(x_1\cdot x_2)(q)}.
\end{equation*}
In particular, setting $x_1 = v $, $x_2 = (g^{-1}h-h',g^{-1})$, we observe that $x_1\cdot x_2 = (g^{-1}h -h,g^{-1})=x^{-1}$ and $x_1^{-1}p = (h-h',1)\cdot (z(h),z)=p'$. Thus, we have the following identity:
\begin{equation}\label{eq: first 2,0}
    \phi^{2,0}_a(v,(g^{-1}h-h',g^{-1}))(p) =\frac{\phi^{1,0}_{a}(v)(p)\cdot \phi^{1,0}_{a}((g^{-1}h-h',g^{-1}))(p')}{\phi^{1,0}_a(x^{-1})(p)} .
\end{equation}
Moreover, swapping the order of the inputs and evaluating at $p'$, we have:
\begin{equation}\label{eq: second 2,0}
    \phi^{2,0}_{a'}((g^{-1}h-h',g^{-1}),v)(p') = \frac{\phi^{1,0}_{a'}((g^{-1}h-h',g^{-1}))(p')\cdot \phi^{1,0}_{ga'}(v)(p)}{\phi^{1,0}_{a'}( (x')^{-1})(p')} 
\end{equation}
where we note that $(g^{-1}h-h',g^{-1})\cdot v = (x')^{-1}$ and $(g^{-1}h-h',g^{-1})^{-1}\cdot p' = (gh'-h,g)\cdot p'=(gz(h),gz)=p\in V_{ga'}$. Combining equations \eqref{eq: first 2,0} and \eqref{eq: second 2,0}, we finally obtain the explicit formula:
\begin{align*}
    \frac{\Phi_{(h,\langle z\rangle,g)}}{\Phi_{(h',\langle z\rangle,g)}}\left(\phi^{1,0},\phi^{0,1}\right) = \frac{\phi^{2,0}_a(v,(g^{-1}h-h',g^{-1}))(p)^{-1}}{ \phi^{2,0}_{a'}((g^{-1}h-h',g^{-1}),v)(p')}\cdot \phi^{1,1}_{a,a'}((g^{-1}h-h',g^{-1}))(p')^{-1}\cdot \phi^{1,1}_{ga',a}(v)(p)\cdot \frac{\phi^{0,2}_{a,ga,ga'}(p)}{\phi^{0,2}_{a,a',ga'}(p')}.
\end{align*}
This completes the proof of the Proposition.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- remark-35: body_md -->
The elements $v=(h'-h,1)$ and $(g^{-1}h-h',g^{-1})^{-1}=(gh'-h,g)$ are precisely the elements which we used to define the $2$-chain whose boundary gave us a homology between the loops associated to $(h,\langle z \rangle,g)$ and $(h',\langle z \rangle,g)$.
<!-- end remark-35 -->
<!-- remark-36: body_md -->
The contribution of $\phi^{1,0}$ term to the evaluation $\Phi_{(h,\langle z \rangle,g)}$ allows us to define a morphism on cochains that descends to cohomology. Additionally, it is a `nicer' formula for the cochain $(\Delta^f,\Gamma)$ in the sense that now $\frac{\Phi_{(h,\langle z\rangle,g)}}{\Phi_{(h',\langle z\rangle,g)}}\left(\Delta^f,\Gamma\right)$ is expressed purely in terms of $D(\Delta^f,\Gamma)$. By adding a redundant $\Delta^f$ term, the change of framing term that previously appeared is now absorbed into the cocycle expression.
<!-- end remark-36 -->
<!-- proposition-20: body_md -->
For $N\in \mathbb{Z}$ and $\big(\begin{smallmatrix}a& b \\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\big)\in\Gamma_0(N)$, then:
    \begin{equation*}
        \frac{\theta_0^N(x,\tau)}{\theta_0^N\left(\frac{x}{c\tau+d},\frac{a\tau+b}{c\tau+d}\right)}\in \mu_{24}.
    \end{equation*} 
    More precisely, the root of unity ambiguity lies in $\mu_{k}$ where $k = \operatorname{gcd}_{(l,N)=1}(l^2-1)$ which we compute to be: 
    \begin{equation*}
        k=\begin{cases}
            \text{  }1 &:\text{  } (N,6)=1 \\
            \text{  }3 &: \text{  }2\nmid N, \text{  }3\mid N \\
            \text{  }8 &: \text{  }2\mid N, \text{             }3\nmid N \\
            \text{  }24 &: \text{  }6|N
        \end{cases}
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end proposition-20 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
$\theta_0^N$ is a meromorphic section of the line bundle $\mathcal{L}$:
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathcal{L}=\begin{cases}
            \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{E}}&: (N,2)=1\\\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{E}}([1/2])&: 2|N 
        \end{cases}
    \end{equation*}
    Moreover, for $g \in\Gamma_0(N)$, we have $g^{*}\theta_0^N$ is a section of the same line bundle $\mathcal{L}$.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
We compute the divisor:
    \begin{equation*}
        \text{div}(\theta_0^N) = N\cdot [\mathcal{O}]-\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\left[\frac{j}{N}\right]
    \end{equation*}
    from which the results follows from an application of Wilson's theorem: namely the sum of these divisors is either $[\mathcal{O}]$ or the unique element of order $2$ when it exists. The claim for $g^*\theta_0^N$ follows immediately from the fact that $\Gamma_0(N)$ preserves $\mathcal{L}$ in either case.
    
    The above only specifies the isomorphsim class of the line bundle $\mathcal{L}$. To see the stronger claim that both $\theta_0^N$ and $g^*\theta_0^N$ are sections of the same line bundle, we explicitly verify they both define the same $\mathbb{Z}^2$-cocycle:
    \begin{align*}
        \theta_0^N(x+1,\tau)=\theta_0^N(x,\tau) &\quad \theta_0^N(x+\tau,\tau)= (-1)^{N-1}\cdot \theta_0^N(x,\tau) \\ g^*\theta_0^N(x+1,\tau)=g^*\theta_0^N(x,\tau) &\quad g^*\theta_0^N(x+\tau,\tau)= (-1)^{N-1}
        \cdot g^*\theta_0^N(x,\tau)
    \end{align*}
    which hold for $g\in \Gamma_0(2)\supset \Gamma_0(N)$. In particular, since these sections square to functions on the universal elliptic curve, it is clear that the line bundle $\mathcal{L}$ must be $2$-torsion.
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
The quotient $\theta_0^N/g^*\theta_0^N$ is a non-vanishing function on $\mathbb{H}$ for $g\in \Gamma_0(N)$.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
In the previous Lemma, we saw $d\theta_0^N = dg^*\theta_0^N\in Z^1(\mathbb{Z}^2,\mathcal{O}^*(\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{H}))$ and so $\theta_0^N/g^*\theta_0^N\in \mathcal{M}^*(\mathcal{E})$. Moreover, for $g\in \Gamma_0(N)$, we compute $\text{div}(g^{*}\theta_0^N)=g^*\text{div}(\theta_0^N)=\text{div}(\theta_0^N)$ and so $\theta_0^N/g^*\theta_0^N\in \mathcal{O}^*(\mathcal{E})=\mathcal{O}^*(\mathbb{H})$.
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
Suppose $g\in \Gamma_0(N)$. Then, as meromorphic functions on $\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{H}$, for all positive integers $(l,N)=1$:
    \begin{align*}
        \prod_{m,n=0}^{l-1}\theta_0^N\left(x+\frac{m\tau+n}{l},\tau\right) = \theta_0^N(lx,\tau)
        \quad \prod_{m,n=0}^{l-1}g^*\theta_0^N\left(x+\frac{m\tau+n}{l},\tau\right) = g^*\theta_0^N(lx,\tau)
    \end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
Since $\theta_0^N=\theta_0/N^*\theta_0$, it remains to show the analogous relation for $N^*\theta_0$. Explicitly:
    \begin{align*}
        \prod_{m,n=0}^{l-1}N^*\theta_0\left(x+\frac{m\tau+n}{l},\tau\right)&= \prod_{m,n=0}^{l-1}\theta_0\left(Nx+\frac{mM\tau+Nn}{l},N\tau\right)\\&=\prod_{m,n=0}^{l-1}\theta_0\left(Nx+\frac{mN\tau+n}{l},N\tau\right)=\theta_0(lNx,N\tau) =N^*\theta_0(lx,\tau) 
    \end{align*}
    where the first and last equalities are definitions. The penultimate equality is \eqref{eq: theta pushforward}. The second equality follows from $N\in (\mathbb{Z}/l)^*$ and $\theta_0(x+1,\tau)=\theta_0(x,\tau)$. This proves the first functional relation.

    Before proving the second relation, we note that if $(N,2)=1$, then it immediately follows from the first one: in this case, we know $\theta_0^N(-,\tau)$ is a function on the elliptic curve $\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}\tau$ and then the first relation can be rephrased as pushforward invariance $[l]_*\theta_0^N = \theta_0^N$. Then, we have $[l]_*g^*\theta_0^N = g^*[l]_*\theta_0^N=g^*\theta_0^N$ since $g$ preserves the $l$-torsion.

    So let us assume $2|N$ and write $g^{
    -1} =\big(\begin{smallmatrix}a& b \\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\big) $. Then, the left hand side is:
    \begin{equation*}
        \prod_{m,n=0}^{l-1}\theta_0^N\left(\frac{x}{c\tau+d}+\frac{m\tau+n}{l(c\tau+d)},\frac{a\tau+b}{c\tau+d}\right)=\prod_{m,n=0}^{l-1}\theta_0^N\left(w+\frac{(dm-cn)\sigma+(-bm+an)}{l},\sigma\right)
    \end{equation*}
    where $w=\frac{x}{c\tau+d}$ and $\sigma = \frac{a\tau+n}{c\tau+d}$. Though we know the product ranges over a set of representatives for the $l$-torsion on $\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}\sigma$, we can no longer conclude as $\theta_0^N$ is not $\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}\sigma$-invariant. Instead, we use the identities:
    \begin{equation*}
        \theta_0^N(x+1,\tau)=\theta_0^N(x,\tau) \quad \theta_0^N(x+\tau,\tau)= (-1)^{N-1}\cdot \theta_0^N(x,\tau) 
    \end{equation*}
    to deduce:
    \begin{align*}
        \prod_{m,n=0}^{l-1}\theta_0^N\left(w+\frac{(dm-cn)\sigma+(-bm+an)}{l},\sigma\right) &= \prod_{m,n=0}^{l-1}(-1)^{x_{m,n}\cdot(N-1)}\theta_0^N\left(w+\frac{m\sigma+n}{l},\sigma\right)\\ &= \prod_{m,n=0}^{l-1}(-1)^{x_{m,n}}\cdot \theta_0^N(lw,\sigma) = (-1)^{\sum x_{m,n}}\cdot g^*\theta_0^N(lx,\tau)
    \end{align*}
    where $x_{m,n}=\frac{1}{l}(dm-cn - [dm-cn]_l)$. It remains to show $\sum{x_{m,n}}\in 2\mathbb{Z}$. We compute:
    \begin{equation*}
       \sum_{m,n=0}^{l-1}{x_{m,n}} = \frac{1}{l}\left(ld\cdot \sum_{m=0}^{l-1}m-lc\cdot\sum_{n=0}^{n-1}n-l\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}k\right)  = \sum_{m=0}^{l-1}m\cdot (d-1-c)\overset{?}{\in}2\mathbb{Z}
    \end{equation*}
    Since we are in the case $N|2$, it follows $g\in \Gamma_0(2)$. In particular, $2|c$ and $(2,d)=1$, so that $2|d-1-c$.
<!-- end proof-57 -->
<!-- corollary-14: body_md -->
For each $\tau\in \mathbb{H}$, the function $\theta_0^N/g^*\theta_0^N(-,\tau)$ on the elliptic curve $\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}\tau$ is invariant under pushforward by $[l]_*$ for all positive integers $l$ such that $(l,N)=1$.
<!-- end corollary-14 -->
<!-- proof-58: body_md -->
Combining the above Lemmas, we know that for $g\in \Gamma_0(N)$ and fixed $\tau$, the quotient $\theta_0^N/g^*\theta_0^N(-,\tau)=\lambda$ for $\lambda\in \mathbb{C}$ satisfying:
    \begin{equation*}
        [l]_*\lambda = \lambda^{l^2}=\lambda\iff  \lambda\in \mu_{l^2-1}  \end{equation*}
    for all $(l,N)=1$. In particular, $\theta_0^N/g^*\theta_0^N(-,\tau)\in \mu_{k}$ for $k=\operatorname{gcd}_{(l,N)=1}(l^2-1)$. The second part of the Proposition, namely the formula for $k$, follows from weak approximation together with the observations:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $(\mathbb{Z}_2^*)^2=1+8\mathbb{Z}_2$. In particular, there exists $t_2\in\mathbb{Z}_2^*$ such that $v_2(t_2^2-1)=3$. 
        \item $(\mathbb{Z}_3^*)^2=1+3\mathbb{Z}_3$. In particular, there exists $t_3\in\mathbb{Z}_3^*$ such that $v_3(t_3^2-1)=1$.
        \item For $p\neq 2,3$, we have $(\mathbb{Z}_p^*)^2=(\mathbb{F}_p^*)^2\cdot 1+p\mathbb{Z}_p$ and $(\mathbb{F}_p^*)^2\neq\{1\}$. In particular, there exists $t_p\in\mathbb{Z}_p^*$ such that $v_p(t_p^2-1)=0$.
    \end{itemize}

    Finally, by the discreteness of $\mu_{24}$, we deduce the result for all $\tau$, namely that $\theta_0^N/g^*\theta_0^N\in \mu_{24}$.
<!-- end proof-58 -->
<!-- remark-37: body_md -->
\label{remark: kato perspective}
    The style of argumentation above leads us to the following characterisation of $\theta_0$. It is the unique holomorphic function on $\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{H}$ that satisfies the pushforward relation \eqref{eq: theta pushforward} and descends to a section of a specified line bundle on $\mathcal{E}$ with divisor $ [\mathcal{O}]$. Immediately, one deduces that $\theta_0/g^*\theta_0\in \mathcal{O}^*(\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{H}) = \exp(\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{H}))$ for $g\in \operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ as pullback by $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ preserves the divisor of the section. The exact form of this automorphy factor, as stated in Lemma \ref{lemma: explicit cocycle j}, can then be deduced by the uniqueness property.
<!-- end remark-37 -->
<!-- corollary-15: body_md -->
The smoothed elliptic Gamma cochain $(\widetilde{\Delta}^{\underline{f}},\widetilde{\Gamma})\in C^1_G(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{M}^*)$ is independent of a compatible pair $\underline{f}$ up to $\mu_{24}$: that is to say $\widetilde{\psi^{\underline{f},\underline{f'}}}\in \mu_{24}$. Moreover, for any compatible pair $\underline{f}$:
    \begin{equation*}
        D(\widetilde{\Delta}^{\underline{f}},\widetilde{\Gamma})=\left(\widetilde{\phi^{2,0}},\widetilde{\phi^{1,1}}\Big\vert_{\mathcal{W}},\widetilde{\phi^{0,2}}\Big\vert_{\mathcal{Q}}\right) \in \mu_{24\cdot N^2}.
    \end{equation*}
    If $(N,6)=1$, then this root of unity is always $1$.
<!-- end corollary-15 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{theorem: total theorem}
    Consider a pair of lattices $(V,L)$ with cyclic quotient $V/L \cong \mathbb{Z}/N$. Consider triples $h\in L\otimes\mathbb{Q}$, $\langle z\rangle \in \mathbb{P}(L^{\vee}\otimes\mathbb{C})-\mathbb{P}(L^{\vee}\otimes\mathbb{R}) $, and an automorphism $g$ of the pair $(V,L)$, that are admissible for the pair $(V,L)$:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $g\cdot h\equiv h$ modulo $L$.
        \item $\langle h\rangle_{\mathbb{Q}}$ generates the quotient $V/L$.
        \item $g\cdot \langle z\rangle =\langle z\rangle$.
    \end{itemize}
    Then for all admissible triples $(h,\langle z \rangle,g)$, $(h',\langle z \rangle,g)$ for the pair $(V,L)$ such that $h\equiv h'$ modulo $L$ and $d(h,h')=3$:
    \begin{equation*}
        \frac{\widetilde{\Phi}(h,\langle z \rangle,g)}{ \widetilde{\Phi}(h',\langle z \rangle,g)}\in \mu_{24\cdot N^2}
    \end{equation*}
    where:
    \begin{equation*}
        \widetilde{\Phi}(h,\langle z \rangle,g)=\widetilde{\Gamma}_{a,ga}(z(h),z)=\frac{\Gamma_{a,ga}(z(h),z;L)^N}{\Gamma_{a,ga}(z(h),z;V)}
    \end{equation*}
    for primitive functional $a\in V^{\vee}$ determined by the triple.

    Moreover, if $(N,6)=1$, then we can strengthen the result in two directions: firstly, this root of unity is always $1$; secondly, if we further assume $(N,\operatorname{disc} (\chi_g))=1$, then we can remove the $d=3$ assumption by always finding an admissible triple $(h'',\langle z \rangle,g)$ with $h''\equiv h'\equiv h$ modulo $L$ such that $d(h,h'')=d(h',h'')=3$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proposition-21: body_md -->
\label{prop: h in L}
    Suppose $g\cdot z=\lambda z$ for $z\in \Lambda\otimes\mathbb{C}-\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{R}$. Then, for all $h\in L$ such that $\langle h \rangle_{\mathbb{Q}}$ generates $V/L$:
    \begin{equation*}
        \widetilde{\Phi}(h,\langle z \rangle,g)^2 = \lambda^{N-1}.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end proposition-21 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
Suppose $g\cdot z=\lambda z$ for $z\in \Lambda\otimes\mathbb{C}-\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{R}$. Then, for $(a,ga)\in\mathcal{W}$:
    \begin{equation*}
        \widetilde{\Gamma}_{a,ga}(0,z)^2=\lambda^{N-1}.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-59: body_md -->
With no assumption on the pair $(a,b)$, we have the completely general equality:
    \begin{equation*}
        \Gamma_{a,b}(w,z)\cdot \Gamma_{a,b}(-w,z)=\frac{\theta_0\left(\frac{w}{z(\gamma)},\frac{z(-\alpha)}{z(\gamma)}\right)}{\theta_0\left(\frac{w}{z(\gamma)},\frac{z(\beta)}{z(\gamma)}\right)}
    \end{equation*}
    for any choice of $(\alpha,\beta)$ that is minimal in the sense discussed in Remark \ref{remark: alpha and beta}. Let $b=ga$ and assume $(a,b)\in\mathcal{W}$. Thus, the smoothed elliptic Gamma is a product of $N$-smoothed $\Gamma$ functions and so we deduce:
    \begin{equation*}
        \widetilde{\Gamma}_{a,b}(w,z)\cdot \widetilde{\Gamma}_{a,b}(-w,z)=\frac{\theta_0^N\left(\frac{w}{z(\gamma)},\frac{z(-\alpha)}{z(\gamma)}\right)}{\theta_0^N\left(\frac{w}{z(\gamma)},\frac{z(\beta)}{z(\gamma)}\right)}.
    \end{equation*}
    Combining $g:\ker(a)\xrightarrow{\sim}\ker(b)$ with $z$ an eigenvector of $g$, yields $\frac{z(\beta)}{z(\gamma)}=\frac{z(g\beta)}{z(g\gamma)} = \delta\cdot \frac{z(-\alpha)}{z(\gamma)}$,
    for some $\delta=\big(\begin{smallmatrix}
        a&b\\c&d
    \end{smallmatrix}\big)\in \Gamma_0(N)$. In particular, $g\gamma = c(-\alpha)+d\gamma$ so that $cz(-\alpha)+dz(\gamma)=z(g\gamma)=g^{-1}z(\gamma)=\lambda^{-1}z(\gamma)$. By $\Gamma_0(N)$-invariance:
    \begin{equation*}
        \theta_0^N\left(\frac{w}{z(\gamma)},\frac{z(-\alpha)}{z(\gamma)}\right) = \theta_0^N\left(\frac{w}{cz(-\alpha)+dz(\gamma)},\frac{z(\beta)}{z(\gamma)}\right) =\theta_0^N\left(\lambda\frac{w}{z(\gamma)},\frac{z(\beta)}{z(\gamma)}\right).
    \end{equation*}
    And so:
    \begin{equation*}
        \widetilde{\Gamma}_{a,b}(w,z)\cdot \widetilde{\Gamma}_{a,b}(-w,z)=\frac{\theta_0^N\left(\lambda\frac{w}{z(\gamma)},\frac{z(\beta)}{z(\gamma)}\right) }{\theta_0^N\left(\frac{w}{z(\gamma)},\frac{z(\beta)}{z(\gamma)}\right)}.
    \end{equation*}
    Since $\theta_0^N(-,\tau)$ is a meromorphic function on $\mathbb{C}$ with a zero of order $N-1$ at zero, we know $\lim_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\theta_0^N(\lambda x,\tau)}{\theta_0^N(x,\tau)} = \lambda^{N-1}$ for all $\lambda\in \mathbb{C}^*$. In particular, $\widetilde{\Gamma}_{a,ba}(0,z)^2=\lambda^{N-1}$.
<!-- end proof-59 -->
<!-- proof-60: body_md -->
By the Lemma above, it suffices to show $\widetilde{\Phi}(h,\langle z \rangle,g) = \widetilde{\Gamma}_{a,ga}(z(h),z)\overset{?}{=}\widetilde{\Gamma}_{a,ga}(0,z)$. From the description of $\Gamma_{a,b}(w,z)$ as a product of standard elliptic Gamma, it is clear that $\Gamma_{a,b}(w,z)$ is invariant under translating $w$ by $\mathbb{Z}\cdot z(\gamma)$. By construction, $\gamma$ is a (positive) primitive vector in the line $\langle h \rangle_{\mathbb{Q}}\cap L$. Thus, when $h\in L$, it follows that $h$ is an \textit{integer} multiple of $\gamma$, which completes the proof of the Proposition.
<!-- end proof-60 -->
